column1: AQA English Language Paper 1 Q1: what is the task and how many marks?
column2:
List four things about a specified part of the source. 4 marks. Stay strictly inside the given line numbers and do not analyse.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 1 Section A: Reading Fiction

column1: What does Paper 1 Q3 ask you to analyse?
column2:
Structure: how the writer has structured the text to interest the reader - the opening focus, changes of focus, and the ending. 8 marks.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 1 Section A: Reading Fiction

column1: Which part of the source must Paper 1 Q4 focus on?
column2:
The second part of the source only (the lines named in the question), evaluating how far you agree with a given statement. 20 marks.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 1 Section A: Reading Fiction

column1: Name three structural features you can write about in Q3.
column2:
Shifts in focus (wide to narrow), time shifts or flashback, cyclical structure, foreshadowing, paragraph length changes, a final revelation.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 1 Section A: Reading Fiction

column1: What is the difference between language and structure analysis?
column2:
Language = choices at word, phrase and sentence level. Structure = the order and shape of ideas across the whole extract.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 1 Section A: Reading Fiction

column1: How are the 40 marks split in Paper 1 Section B?
column2:
24 marks for content and organisation, 16 marks for technical accuracy (SPaG, sentence variety, vocabulary range).

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 1 Section B: Descriptive and Narrative Writing

column1: How long should you spend on Paper 1 Section B?
column2:
About 45 minutes: 5 minutes planning, 35 minutes writing, 5 minutes proofreading.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 1 Section B: Descriptive and Narrative Writing

column1: Give three techniques that lift a descriptive piece into the top band.
column2:
Extended metaphor sustained across paragraphs, deliberate one-sentence paragraph for impact, and shifting sensory focus rather than listing adjectives.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 1 Section B: Descriptive and Narrative Writing

column1: Why is a cyclical structure useful in the narrative task?
column2:
It shows deliberate crafting and gives a controlled ending, which the mark scheme rewards under organisation.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 1 Section B: Descriptive and Narrative Writing

column1: Which Paper 2 question carries the most marks and what does it require?
column2:
Q4, 16 marks: compare how the two writers convey their different attitudes or perspectives, analysing methods and using evidence from both sources.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 2 Section A: Reading Non-Fiction

column1: What is the key skill in Paper 2 Q2?
column2:
Synthesis and inference - combining information from both sources and drawing conclusions, not just quoting.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 2 Section A: Reading Non-Fiction

column1: Paper 2 Q3 is worth how many marks and covers how many sources?
column2:
12 marks, one source only, focused on how language is used to achieve a stated purpose.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 2 Section A: Reading Non-Fiction

column1: Give two useful comparison connectives for Q4.
column2:
Whereas, by contrast, in a similar way, conversely, on the other hand.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 2 Section A: Reading Non-Fiction

column1: What does DAFOREST stand for?
column2:
Direct address, Anecdote, Facts, Opinion, Rhetorical question, Emotive language, Statistics, Triples (rule of three).

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 2 Section B: Writing to Present a Viewpoint

column1: Why include a counter-argument in Paper 2 Section B?
column2:
Acknowledging then refuting an opposing view shows a sophisticated, controlled argument, which is required for the top content band.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 2 Section B: Writing to Present a Viewpoint

column1: If the question asks for a letter, what two conventions must appear?
column2:
An appropriate salutation (Dear Sir or Madam / Dear Mr Smith) and a matching sign-off (Yours faithfully / Yours sincerely).

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 2 Section B: Writing to Present a Viewpoint

column1: What is the mark split for Paper 2 Section B?
column2:
24 marks content and organisation, 16 marks technical accuracy - the same as Paper 1 Section B.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Paper 2 Section B: Writing to Present a Viewpoint

column1: Does the Spoken Language endorsement affect the GCSE English Language grade?
column2:
No. It is separately endorsed and reported as Pass, Merit, Distinction or Not Classified alongside the 9-1 grade.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Spoken Language Endorsement

column1: What three things are assessed in the Spoken Language endorsement?
column2:
Presenting information and ideas, responding to questions and feedback, and using Standard English.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Spoken Language Endorsement

column1: When do you use a semicolon rather than a comma?
column2:
To join two closely related independent clauses that could each stand alone as a sentence.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Technical Accuracy Toolkit

column1: What does the paragraphing rule TipTop stand for?
column2:
Start a new paragraph when there is a change of Time, Place, Topic or Person.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Technical Accuracy Toolkit

column1: Explain the difference between affect and effect.
column2:
Affect is usually a verb (to influence); effect is usually a noun (the result).

English Language · AQA 8700 · Technical Accuracy Toolkit

column1: What is a minor sentence and why use one?
column2:
A grammatically incomplete sentence, e.g. Silence. Used sparingly for dramatic emphasis.

English Language · AQA 8700 · Technical Accuracy Toolkit

column1: Why did Priestley set An Inspector Calls in 1912 but write it in 1945?
column2:
To use dramatic irony: the 1945 audience knew the 1912 optimism about peace and prosperity (and the Titanic) was about to be shattered, reinforcing his warning against complacency.

English Literature · OCR J352 · An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)

column1: How does Sheila change across the play?
column2:
She moves from a spoilt, jealous fiancee in Act One to the character who most fully accepts responsibility and challenges her parents' refusal to learn, showing Priestley's hope for the younger generation.

English Literature · OCR J352 · An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)

column1: What is the dramatic function of the Inspector's exit speech?
column2:
It delivers Priestley's central socialist message directly to the audience: that if people do not learn collective responsibility, the world faces 'fire and blood and anguish' - a warning about war.

English Literature · OCR J352 · An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)

column1: Why does Priestley never let Eva Smith appear on stage?
column2:
It keeps the focus on how each character treats her, turning her into a symbol of the invisible, exploited working class rather than an individual the audience can dismiss.

English Literature · OCR J352 · An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)

column1: What is significant about the play's final telephone call?
column2:
It repeats the opening announcement almost exactly, creating a cyclical structure that suggests the family's chance to learn may be about to repeat, or that they cannot escape the consequences of their actions.

English Literature · OCR J352 · An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)

column1: How does Mr Birling's dramatic irony work in Act One?
column2:
His confident, factually wrong predictions (Titanic 'unsinkable', no war coming) immediately undermine his authority for the audience, discrediting his capitalist worldview from the start.

English Literature · OCR J352 · An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)

column1: What does Gerald's reaction to the Inspector possibly being fake reveal?
column2:
His relief shows he wants to escape moral responsibility rather than learn from what happened, aligning him with the older generation despite his youth.

English Literature · OCR J352 · An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)

column1: What does the surname 'Goole' suggest about the Inspector?
column2:
It sounds like 'ghoul', hinting he may be supernatural, a moral force, or Eva's avenging conscience rather than a literal police inspector.

English Literature · OCR J352 · An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)

column1: Give two ways stagecraft controls mood in the play.
column2:
The single continuous set keeps tension concentrated in one room, and the lighting shifts from 'pink and intimate' to 'brighter and harder' when the Inspector arrives, exposing the family.

English Literature · OCR J352 · An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)

column1: What is the central thematic conflict of the play?
column2:
Individual responsibility and capitalism (the Birlings' view) versus collective responsibility and socialism (the Inspector's view), reflecting Priestley's own political beliefs.

English Literature · OCR J352 · An Inspector Calls (Component 01, Section A)

column1: What is the central duality explored in Jekyll and Hyde?
column2:
Stevenson presents every person as containing both a civilised, respectable self and a primitive, immoral self - 'man is not truly one, but truly two'.

English Literature · OCR J352 · The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)

column1: Why does Stevenson delay revealing that Jekyll and Hyde are the same person?
column2:
The novel is structured as a mystery; withholding the connection builds suspense and lets the reader experience Utterson's own confusion and investigation.

English Literature · OCR J352 · The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)

column1: What is the effect of using multiple narrators (Utterson, Lanyon's letter, Jekyll's confession)?
column2:
Each narrator has a different degree of knowledge and reliability, gradually revealing more of the truth and letting Stevenson delay full disclosure until the very end.

English Literature · OCR J352 · The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)

column1: How is Hyde physically described, and why?
column2:
As smaller, ape-like and giving an instinctive impression of deformity - his appearance reflects an atavistic, animalistic morality, tying into Victorian anxiety about evolution.

English Literature · OCR J352 · The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)

column1: Why does Dr Lanyon die after witnessing the transformation?
column2:
As a rational man of science, witnessing Hyde transform into Jekyll shatters his entire scientific worldview - the shock destroys him.

English Literature · OCR J352 · The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)

column1: What does the locked door and Jekyll's cabinet symbolise?
column2:
The barrier between Jekyll's respectable public life and his hidden, secret self - a physical symbol of Victorian double lives.

English Literature · OCR J352 · The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)

column1: How does the novel reflect Victorian anxieties about respectability?
column2:
Jekyll's fear of public disgrace drives him to create Hyde as an outlet for desires he cannot express respectably, mirroring real Victorian fears of hidden vice behind a public facade.

English Literature · OCR J352 · The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)

column1: What role does fog play in the novel's setting?
column2:
It is a Gothic device that obscures and disorientates, mirroring the moral confusion and hidden truths at the heart of the story, and reflects real Victorian London smog.

English Literature · OCR J352 · The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)

column1: How does Jekyll lose control over his transformations?
column2:
What begins as a deliberate, controlled experiment becomes involuntary - Hyde starts to emerge without the potion, showing addiction and the danger of indulging one's darker nature.

English Literature · OCR J352 · The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)

column1: What is significant about Jekyll's final written confession?
column2:
It is the only first-person account in the novel, finally giving the reader Jekyll's own motives, guilt and admission that he created Hyde to escape moral responsibility for his vices.

English Literature · OCR J352 · The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (Component 01, Section B)

column1: Why might Shakespeare have written Macbeth to flatter King James I?
column2:
James I believed in the divine right of kings and claimed descent from Banquo; the play condemns regicide and shows witchcraft (a subject James wrote about) as a real, dangerous force.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)

column1: How does Macbeth change from Act 1 to Act 5?
column2:
He moves from a brave, loyal general praised by the Sergeant to a paranoid tyrant who murders friends and children, showing the corrupting effect of unchecked ambition.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)

column1: What is the dramatic function of Macbeth's soliloquies?
column2:
They reveal his internal conflict between ambition and conscience, letting the audience see the moral cost of his actions that other characters cannot.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)

column1: How does Lady Macbeth manipulate Macbeth before Duncan's murder?
column2:
She questions his masculinity and courage, telling him to 'screw your courage to the sticking-place', pushing him past his own doubts.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)

column1: Trace the blood motif across the play.
column2:
Macbeth is first praised for his bloody, heroic actions in battle; after Duncan's murder blood becomes a symbol of guilt, culminating in Lady Macbeth's hallucinated bloodstains she cannot wash away.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)

column1: What does Banquo's ghost at the banquet represent?
column2:
Macbeth's guilty conscience made visible - only he can see the ghost, showing his growing psychological disintegration and isolation.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)

column1: How does Shakespeare use the natural world to reflect the murder of Duncan?
column2:
Unnatural disorder follows the regicide - storms, strange animal behaviour and darkness during daytime - reflecting the Jacobean belief that killing a king disrupted the natural and divine order.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)

column1: What is Macduff's dramatic role in the play?
column2:
He is the avenging hero who loses his family to Macbeth's tyranny and ultimately kills Macbeth, restoring rightful order under Malcolm.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)

column1: Do the witches control Macbeth's fate, or reveal his own ambition?
column2:
This is deliberately ambiguous - the prophecy could be read as manipulating him, or simply voicing an ambition that was already within him, which he then chooses to act on.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)

column1: What does the sleepwalking scene reveal about Lady Macbeth?
column2:
Unlike her earlier confident ruthlessness, she is now consumed by guilt she cannot control or voice while awake, showing psychological collapse.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Macbeth (Component 02, Section B)

column1: How is the Poetry Anthology question on Component 02 structured?
column2:
One named poem from your studied cluster is printed on the paper alongside a linked unseen poem; you compare how both poems present a given theme, focusing on methods.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships Cluster

column1: Why does this revision set avoid naming specific poems in the Love and Relationships cluster?
column2:
The family has not confirmed which OCR poetry cluster is studied, and the specific poem list has not been independently verified, so guessing titles risks embedding wrong facts - only certain themes and methods are covered.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships Cluster

column1: What comparative approach should you use regardless of which poems appear?
column2:
Identify a shared idea or theme first, then compare each poet's methods (form, structure, imagery, tone) for presenting it, rather than describing each poem separately.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships Cluster

column1: Why is the sonnet form often associated with love poetry?
column2:
Its traditional 14-line structure and volta (turn) suit exploring a single idea about love and then complicating or resolving it, a pattern many love poems adapt or subvert.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships Cluster

column1: What is a dramatic monologue and why might it suit a love poem?
column2:
A poem spoken in a single created voice, which can reveal a speaker's feelings about a relationship more intimately, including feelings they may not fully realise themselves.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships Cluster

column1: Give an example of how imagery might mirror a relationship in a love poem.
column2:
Nature imagery (blossoming, withering) can mirror the growth or decline of feeling, while domestic imagery can convey intimacy or entrapment within a relationship.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships Cluster

column1: How can rhyme and rhythm reflect the state of a relationship?
column2:
A regular, harmonious rhyme scheme can suggest a stable or contented relationship, while broken rhythm, irregular line lengths or free verse can suggest conflict or emotional turmoil.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships Cluster

column1: What is the risk of comparing two poems 'poem by poem'?
column2:
It tends to become description of each poem in turn rather than sustained comparison, which limits marks for comparative analysis of methods.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Love and Relationships Cluster

column1: What kinds of conflict might appear across poems in this cluster?
column2:
Physical war and battle, the psychological aftermath of conflict for soldiers or civilians, conflict between generations or cultures, and inner emotional conflict.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Conflict Cluster

column1: Why might a poet use fragmented or disrupted structure in a conflict poem?
column2:
To mirror the chaos, disorientation or trauma of conflict, rather than presenting events in a calm, orderly way.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Conflict Cluster

column1: How can caesura be used effectively in a conflict poem?
column2:
A sudden pause mid-line can convey shock, interruption, or a sudden violent event, forcing the reader to pause as the speaker might.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Conflict Cluster

column1: What is the effect of contrasting imagery of home or peace within a conflict poem?
column2:
It heightens the horror or loss of conflict by reminding the reader what has been destroyed or is unreachable, creating emotional contrast.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Conflict Cluster

column1: Why might a poet choose a restrained, controlled tone to describe violence?
column2:
Understatement can be more powerful than explicit horror, letting the facts or images speak for themselves and inviting the reader to supply the emotional response.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Conflict Cluster

column1: What should you compare when two conflict poems share a similar theme, such as loss?
column2:
Not just that both mention loss, but how each poet's structure, imagery, form and tone create a different presentation or attitude towards that loss.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Conflict Cluster

column1: Give an example of a sound device used for violent effect in conflict poetry.
column2:
Harsh plosive consonants (b, p, k, t) can mimic gunfire, explosions or physical blows, adding a visceral quality to the language.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Conflict Cluster

column1: Why is identifying the poet's attitude to conflict part of a strong comparison?
column2:
Poems on conflict can glorify, question, mourn or condemn war differently; naming that stance sharpens the comparison beyond just shared subject matter.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Conflict Cluster

column1: What kinds of relationships or experiences might feature in a Youth and Age cluster?
column2:
Childhood memory, generational relationships such as parent/child or grandparent/grandchild, the loss of innocence, ageing and mortality, and nostalgia for the past.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Youth and Age Cluster

column1: Why might a poet use a shift between past and present tense in a poem about memory?
column2:
It can show the gap between how something felt at the time and how it is remembered or understood now, highlighting change or loss.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Youth and Age Cluster

column1: How can seasonal imagery be used to represent stages of life?
column2:
Spring or summer can represent youth and growth, while autumn or winter can represent ageing, decline or approaching death.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Youth and Age Cluster

column1: What might a circular (returning) structure suggest in a poem about memory?
column2:
That the speaker is unable to move on from a particular moment, or that the memory continues to shape the present.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Youth and Age Cluster

column1: Give an example of an object that might symbolise the passage of time in this cluster.
column2:
A photograph, an old house or an item of clothing can outlast the people connected to it, symbolising memory, loss or the passing of time.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Youth and Age Cluster

column1: How might tone shift across a poem about ageing or childhood?
column2:
It might move from nostalgic warmth to regret, or from innocence to a more painful adult understanding, and identifying that shift is valuable for analysis.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Youth and Age Cluster

column1: What should a comparison of two poems on this theme focus on beyond shared subject matter?
column2:
How each poet's structure, imagery, tense and tone create a different attitude towards time, memory or the relationship being described.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Youth and Age Cluster

column1: Why is an irregular poetic form sometimes suited to a poem about memory?
column2:
It can suggest memory's unreliability or fragmented nature, contrasting with a tight, regular form that might suggest a controlled, ordered recollection.

English Literature · OCR J352 · OCR Poetry Anthology: Youth and Age Cluster

column1: Why must quotations be memorised for both OCR Literature components?
column2:
Both components are closed text exams - no copies of the studied texts are permitted in the exam room.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352

column1: What is assessed by AO3 in OCR GCSE English Literature?
column2:
Understanding of the relationship between texts and the contexts in which they were written, worth 15% of the whole qualification overall - less than AO1 or AO2.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352

column1: In which sections is AO4 assessed?
column2:
Only in Section B of each component (19th century prose in Component 01, Shakespeare in Component 02), where it carries a separate small mark allocation for spelling, punctuation and sentence variety.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352

column1: What does the Point-Method-Effect paragraph structure mean?
column2:
State the point you are making, show the method the writer uses with embedded evidence, then explain the effect on the reader or meaning and link back to the question.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352

column1: Why is embedding quotations better than dropping them into a separate sentence?
column2:
It keeps the sentence fluent and lets you analyse individual words precisely within your own argument, which is exactly what AO2 rewards.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352

column1: How should you approach the extract in a 19th century prose or Shakespeare question?
column2:
Analyse the extract closely first, since it is the anchor for the whole answer, before ranging outward to make links with the rest of the text.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352

column1: Roughly how much time should you spend on each 40-mark section in a 2-hour paper?
column2:
Around 45-50 minutes each, leaving a short amount of time to check spelling, punctuation and grammar, especially in Section B answers.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352

column1: What should you do in the first few minutes before writing an essay?
column2:
Identify the key words in the question, decide your line of argument (thesis), and jot 3-4 topic sentences to structure your paragraphs.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352

column1: Why weave context into analysis rather than writing a separate context paragraph?
column2:
AO3 rewards context that shapes interpretation of the text, not standalone historical facts disconnected from the question.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352

column1: Give one useful technique for offering deeper analysis of a quotation.
column2:
Zoom in on a single word within the quotation and offer more than one plausible interpretation of its effect or connotation.

English Literature · OCR J352 · Exam Skills and Essay Craft for J352

column1: State the angle at the centre theorem.
column2:
The angle subtended by an arc at the centre of a circle is twice the angle subtended by the same arc at the circumference.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Circle Theorems (KEFW Year 11 Unit 1)

column1: What is the alternate segment theorem?
column2:
The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment subtended by that chord.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Circle Theorems (KEFW Year 11 Unit 1)

column1: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add to what?
column2:
180 degrees.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Circle Theorems (KEFW Year 11 Unit 1)

column1: What angle does a tangent make with the radius at the point of contact?
column2:
90 degrees.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Circle Theorems (KEFW Year 11 Unit 1)

column1: What is special about the angle in a semicircle?
column2:
It is always 90 degrees (the angle subtended by a diameter at the circumference).

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Circle Theorems (KEFW Year 11 Unit 1)

column1: In an exam proof, what must you write alongside each step?
column2:
The name of the theorem or reason used, e.g. angles in the same segment are equal - marks are awarded for reasons, not just values.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Circle Theorems (KEFW Year 11 Unit 1)

column1: How do you find fg(x)?
column2:
Apply g first, then substitute the result into f. Work from the inside out.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Algebra and Functions (KEFW Year 11 Unit 2)

column1: How do you find the inverse of a function f(x)?
column2:
Write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject. That is f inverse of x.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Algebra and Functions (KEFW Year 11 Unit 2)

column1: How do you represent two consecutive even numbers algebraically?
column2:
2n and 2n + 2, where n is an integer.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Algebra and Functions (KEFW Year 11 Unit 2)

column1: How do you show an expression is always a multiple of 4?
column2:
Simplify it into the form 4 times (an integer expression), then state that since the bracket is an integer the whole expression is a multiple of 4.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Algebra and Functions (KEFW Year 11 Unit 2)

column1: First step when simplifying an algebraic fraction like (x squared minus 9)/(x squared + 4x + 3)?
column2:
Factorise fully top and bottom: (x-3)(x+3) over (x+3)(x+1), then cancel the common factor to get (x-3)/(x+1).

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Algebra and Functions (KEFW Year 11 Unit 2)

column1: In iteration, what does the subscript notation x sub n+1 mean?
column2:
The next term in the sequence, generated by substituting the current value x sub n into the iterative formula.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Algebra and Functions (KEFW Year 11 Unit 2)

column1: How do you know two vectors are parallel?
column2:
One is a scalar multiple of the other, e.g. vector b = k times vector a.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Vectors and Geometric Proof (KEFW Year 11 Unit 3)

column1: How do you prove three points A, B and C are collinear using vectors?
column2:
Show that vector AB and vector BC are scalar multiples of each other and share a common point, so they lie on the same straight line.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Vectors and Geometric Proof (KEFW Year 11 Unit 3)

column1: How do you find the magnitude of the column vector (3, 4)?
column2:
Use Pythagoras: square root of (3 squared + 4 squared) = 5.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Vectors and Geometric Proof (KEFW Year 11 Unit 3)

column1: What does the vector AB equal in terms of position vectors a and b?
column2:
Vector AB = b minus a (destination minus start).

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Vectors and Geometric Proof (KEFW Year 11 Unit 3)

column1: If P divides AB in the ratio 2:3, what is vector AP?
column2:
Vector AP = two fifths of vector AB.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Vectors and Geometric Proof (KEFW Year 11 Unit 3)

column1: What does x to the power of negative n equal?
column2:
1 divided by x to the power of n.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Higher Retrieval: Number, Ratio and Proportion

column1: What does x to the power of one third mean?
column2:
The cube root of x.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Higher Retrieval: Number, Ratio and Proportion

column1: How do you rationalise the denominator of 1 over root 3?
column2:
Multiply top and bottom by root 3 to get root 3 over 3.

Mathematics · Pearson Edexcel 1MA1 · Higher Retrieval: Number, Ratio and Proportion

column1: If a value is 15 percent more than the original and equals 92, how do you find the original?
column2:
Reverse percentage: divide by 1.15, giving 80.

Positive: two real roots. Zero: one repeated root. Negative: no real roots.

Negative 3/2 - the negative reciprocal.

A translation of a units in the negative x direction (left if a is positive).

x squared plus y squared equals 25.

a squared = b squared + c squared minus 2bc cos A.

a over sin A = b over sin B = c over sin C.

One half.

1.

Area scale factor 9, volume scale factor 27.

One half times a times b times sin C.

Four thirds times pi times r cubed.

Frequency divided by class width. Needed for histograms with unequal class widths, where area represents frequency.

Read off the upper quartile at 0.75n and the lower quartile at 0.25n, then subtract.

The denominator of the second set of branches decreases by one, because the total has reduced.

The sample is split into groups in the same proportion as the population, then sampled randomly within each group.

It predicts beyond the range of the data, where the observed trend may not continue.

column1: Define a community in ecological terms.
column2:
All the populations of different species living and interacting in the same habitat.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6a Ecology: Adaptations, Communities and Interdependence

column1: Give three abiotic factors that affect a community.
column2:
Light intensity, temperature, moisture level, soil pH and mineral content, wind intensity, carbon dioxide or oxygen levels.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6a Ecology: Adaptations, Communities and Interdependence

column1: Give three biotic factors that affect a community.
column2:
Availability of food, new predators arriving, new pathogens, and interspecific competition.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6a Ecology: Adaptations, Communities and Interdependence

column1: What are extremophiles?
column2:
Organisms adapted to live in extreme conditions such as high temperature, high pressure or high salt concentration, e.g. bacteria in deep sea vents.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6a Ecology: Adaptations, Communities and Interdependence

column1: Why do predator and prey population cycles lag behind each other?
column2:
Predator numbers rise only after prey numbers rise, and prey numbers recover only after predator numbers fall - there is a time delay in each response.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6a Ecology: Adaptations, Communities and Interdependence

column1: What three things do plants compete for?
column2:
Light and space, water, and mineral ions from the soil.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6a Ecology: Adaptations, Communities and Interdependence

column1: What does interdependence mean?
column2:
Species within a community rely on each other for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal, so removing one species affects the whole community.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6a Ecology: Adaptations, Communities and Interdependence

column1: Why must quadrat samples be placed randomly?
column2:
To avoid bias so the sample is representative of the whole area, allowing a valid estimate of the total population.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6b Ecology: Sampling, Cycling of Materials and Decomposition

column1: How do you estimate the total population of a plant from quadrat data?
column2:
Mean number per quadrat divided by quadrat area, multiplied by the total area of the habitat.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6b Ecology: Sampling, Cycling of Materials and Decomposition

column1: When would you use a transect rather than random quadrats?
column2:
When investigating how distribution changes along an environmental gradient, e.g. from the shore inland.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6b Ecology: Sampling, Cycling of Materials and Decomposition

column1: Name the three processes that return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
column2:
Respiration, combustion of fossil fuels and wood, and decomposition by microorganisms.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6b Ecology: Sampling, Cycling of Materials and Decomposition

column1: Which three factors increase the rate of decay?
column2:
Warmer temperature (up to enzyme denaturation), presence of water, and plenty of oxygen for aerobic respiration.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6b Ecology: Sampling, Cycling of Materials and Decomposition

column1: Why does anaerobic decay matter in a biogas generator?
column2:
Anaerobic decay by microorganisms produces methane, which can be burned as a fuel.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6b Ecology: Sampling, Cycling of Materials and Decomposition

column1: How is water made available to living organisms in the water cycle?
column2:
Energy from the Sun evaporates water, which condenses to form clouds and falls as precipitation, providing fresh water on land before draining back to the sea.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6b Ecology: Sampling, Cycling of Materials and Decomposition

column1: Define biodiversity.
column2:
The variety of all the different species of organisms on Earth, or within an ecosystem.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6c Ecology: Biodiversity, Human Impact and Food Production

column1: Why is high biodiversity important?
column2:
It reduces the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment, giving a stable ecosystem.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6c Ecology: Biodiversity, Human Impact and Food Production

column1: Why does destroying peat bogs increase carbon dioxide levels?
column2:
Peat contains large amounts of stored carbon; when it is drained or burned, microorganisms respire it or it combusts, releasing carbon dioxide.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6c Ecology: Biodiversity, Human Impact and Food Production

column1: Give two reasons for large-scale deforestation in tropical areas.
column2:
To provide land for cattle and rice fields, and to grow crops for biofuel production.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6c Ecology: Biodiversity, Human Impact and Food Production

column1: How do you calculate the efficiency of biomass transfer between trophic levels?
column2:
Biomass transferred to the higher level divided by biomass available at the lower level, multiplied by 100.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6c Ecology: Biodiversity, Human Impact and Food Production

column1: Approximately what percentage of biomass is transferred between trophic levels?
column2:
About 10 percent - the rest is lost in faeces, urea, respiration and uneaten parts.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6c Ecology: Biodiversity, Human Impact and Food Production

column1: Name four programmes that help maintain biodiversity.
column2:
Breeding programmes for endangered species, protection and regeneration of rare habitats, field margins and hedgerows on farms, and recycling rather than landfill.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6c Ecology: Biodiversity, Human Impact and Food Production

column1: How is mycoprotein produced?
column2:
The fungus Fusarium is grown on glucose syrup in aerobic conditions in a fermenter; the biomass is harvested and purified as a protein-rich food.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6c Ecology: Biodiversity, Human Impact and Food Production

column1: Give two ways fish stocks are conserved.
column2:
Controlling net mesh size so young fish escape, and imposing fishing quotas that limit catch.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.6c Ecology: Biodiversity, Human Impact and Food Production

column1: How many daughter cells does meiosis produce and how do they differ?
column2:
Four genetically different haploid gametes, each with half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7a Inheritance: Reproduction, DNA and Genetic Crosses

column1: What is the complementary base pair rule in DNA?
column2:
Adenine pairs with thymine, and cytosine pairs with guanine.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7a Inheritance: Reproduction, DNA and Genetic Crosses

column1: Define the genome.
column2:
The entire genetic material of an organism.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7a Inheritance: Reproduction, DNA and Genetic Crosses

column1: What is the difference between transcription and translation?
column2:
Transcription copies a gene into mRNA in the nucleus; translation reads the mRNA on a ribosome, where tRNA brings amino acids in the coded order to build a protein.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7a Inheritance: Reproduction, DNA and Genetic Crosses

column1: Cystic fibrosis is caused by which type of allele?
column2:
A recessive allele - a person must inherit two copies to have the disorder.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7a Inheritance: Reproduction, DNA and Genetic Crosses

column1: Polydactyly is caused by which type of allele?
column2:
A dominant allele - only one copy is needed for the phenotype.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7a Inheritance: Reproduction, DNA and Genetic Crosses

column1: What is the expected ratio from crossing two heterozygous parents (Bb x Bb)?
column2:
3 showing the dominant phenotype to 1 showing the recessive phenotype (genotypes 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb).

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7a Inheritance: Reproduction, DNA and Genetic Crosses

column1: Which chromosomes determine sex in humans?
column2:
XX is female and XY is male; the 23rd pair of chromosomes.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7a Inheritance: Reproduction, DNA and Genetic Crosses

column1: Why is asexual reproduction advantageous in stable conditions?
column2:
It is faster, needs only one parent, and produces many genetically identical offspring adapted to the existing environment.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7a Inheritance: Reproduction, DNA and Genetic Crosses

column1: Define homozygous and heterozygous.
column2:
Homozygous: two identical alleles for a gene. Heterozygous: two different alleles for a gene.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7a Inheritance: Reproduction, DNA and Genetic Crosses

column1: Explain natural selection in four steps.
column2:
Variation exists within a species due to mutation; individuals with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and breed; the beneficial alleles are passed to offspring; over many generations the species changes.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7b Variation, Evolution, Extinction and Classification

column1: Who developed the theory of evolution alongside Darwin?
column2:
Alfred Russel Wallace, who published jointly with Darwin on natural selection in 1858.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7b Variation, Evolution, Extinction and Classification

column1: Why was Darwins theory only gradually accepted?
column2:
It challenged the idea that God created all life; there was insufficient evidence at the time; and the mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years later.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7b Variation, Evolution, Extinction and Classification

column1: Define speciation.
column2:
The formation of a new species when two populations become so different in phenotype that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7b Variation, Evolution, Extinction and Classification

column1: Why is the fossil record incomplete?
column2:
Many early organisms were soft-bodied and left few traces, and many fossils that did form have been destroyed by geological activity.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7b Variation, Evolution, Extinction and Classification

column1: How do bacteria become antibiotic resistant?
column2:
Random mutation produces a resistant strain; the antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria; the resistant strain survives, reproduces rapidly and spreads because there is no effective treatment.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7b Variation, Evolution, Extinction and Classification

column1: List the Linnaean classification groups in order.
column2:
Kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7b Variation, Evolution, Extinction and Classification

column1: What are the three domains proposed by Carl Woese?
column2:
Archaea, bacteria and eukaryota.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7b Variation, Evolution, Extinction and Classification

column1: Give three ways to slow the development of antibiotic resistance.
column2:
Doctors avoid prescribing antibiotics inappropriately, patients complete the full course, and agricultural use of antibiotics is restricted.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7b Variation, Evolution, Extinction and Classification

column1: How does the binomial system name a species?
column2:
By genus then species, e.g. Homo sapiens, with the genus capitalised.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7b Variation, Evolution, Extinction and Classification

column1: Describe the process of selective breeding.
column2:
Choose parents with the desired characteristic, breed them, select the best offspring, then breed those together, repeating over many generations.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7c Selective Breeding, Genetic Engineering and Cloning

column1: What is the main risk of selective breeding?
column2:
Inbreeding reduces the gene pool, so inherited defects become more common and the whole population is vulnerable to a single new disease.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7c Selective Breeding, Genetic Engineering and Cloning

column1: Outline the main steps of genetic engineering.
column2:
Cut out the required gene using enzymes, insert it into a vector such as a bacterial plasmid or a virus, then use the vector to insert the gene into the cells of the target organism at an early stage of development.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7c Selective Breeding, Genetic Engineering and Cloning

column1: Give two arguments for GM crops and two against.
column2:
For: higher yields, added nutrients such as vitamin A in golden rice, and pest resistance reducing pesticide use. Against: possible effects on wild flowers and insect populations, and uncertain long-term effects on human health.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7c Selective Breeding, Genetic Engineering and Cloning

column1: Describe adult cell cloning.
column2:
The nucleus is removed from an unfertilised egg cell; the nucleus from an adult body cell is inserted; the cell is stimulated by an electric shock to divide into an embryo, which is inserted into the womb of an adult female.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7c Selective Breeding, Genetic Engineering and Cloning

column1: What is tissue culture used for?
column2:
Using small groups of cells from a plant to grow identical new plants, useful for preserving rare species or commercially producing large numbers of identical plants.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7c Selective Breeding, Genetic Engineering and Cloning

column1: How are embryo transplants used in cattle farming?
column2:
Cells are split from a developing embryo before they become specialised, and the identical embryos are implanted into host mothers.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461 · B5.7c Selective Breeding, Genetic Engineering and Cloning

column1: What forms at the cathode during electrolysis of molten lead bromide?
column2:
Lead metal, because positive metal ions are attracted to the negative cathode and are reduced.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C4 Chemical Changes Part 2: Electrolysis

column1: State the cathode rule for electrolysis of aqueous solutions.
column2:
Hydrogen is produced unless the metal present is less reactive than hydrogen, in which case the metal is deposited.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C4 Chemical Changes Part 2: Electrolysis

column1: State the anode rule for electrolysis of aqueous solutions.
column2:
Oxygen is produced unless a halide ion is present, in which case the halogen is produced.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C4 Chemical Changes Part 2: Electrolysis

column1: Write the half equation for hydrogen forming at the cathode.
column2:
2H+ plus 2e- gives H2.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C4 Chemical Changes Part 2: Electrolysis

column1: Write the half equation for oxygen forming at the anode from hydroxide ions.
column2:
4OH- gives O2 plus 2H2O plus 4e-.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C4 Chemical Changes Part 2: Electrolysis

column1: Why is cryolite added during aluminium extraction?
column2:
It lowers the melting point of aluminium oxide, reducing the energy and cost required to keep it molten.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C4 Chemical Changes Part 2: Electrolysis

column1: Why can aluminium not be extracted by reduction with carbon?
column2:
Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot displace it from its oxide - electrolysis is required.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C4 Chemical Changes Part 2: Electrolysis

column1: What does OILRIG stand for?
column2:
Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain - of electrons.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C4 Chemical Changes Part 2: Electrolysis

column1: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved for electrolysis?
column2:
The ions must be free to move to the electrodes to carry the charge.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C4 Chemical Changes Part 2: Electrolysis

column1: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
column2:
CnH2n+2.

column1: What is the general formula of the alkenes?

CnH2n.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: Name the first four alkanes.
column2:
Methane, ethane, propane, butane.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: How does fractional distillation separate crude oil?
column2:
Oil is heated and vaporised, then fed into a column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top; each fraction condenses where the temperature matches its boiling point range.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: How does bromine water distinguish an alkane from an alkene?
column2:
Alkenes decolourise orange bromine water to colourless by addition across the double bond; alkanes leave it orange.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: Why is cracking carried out?
column2:
Long-chain fractions are in low demand, so they are broken into shorter, more useful alkanes and into alkenes needed to make polymers.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: Give the conditions for catalytic cracking.
column2:
Heat the long-chain hydrocarbon to vaporise it and pass the vapour over a hot catalyst.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: What is the functional group of a carboxylic acid?
column2:
COOH.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: What are the products when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid?
column2:
An ester and water, using an acid catalyst.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: Give the conditions needed for fermentation.
column2:
Aqueous sugar solution, yeast, warm temperature around 25 to 35 degrees Celsius, and anaerobic conditions.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: How does addition polymerisation differ from condensation polymerisation?
column2:
Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers with no other product; condensation polymerisation joins monomers with two functional groups and loses a small molecule, usually water, each time.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: What are proteins made from?
column2:
Amino acid monomers joined by condensation polymerisation into polypeptides.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: How do boiling point and viscosity change as hydrocarbon chains get longer?
column2:
Both increase, while flammability decreases.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C7 Organic Chemistry
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C7_Organic_Chemistry AQA::8462 Basic

column1: How is Rf value calculated?
column2:
Distance moved by the substance divided by the distance moved by the solvent front.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: What is a formulation?
column2:
A mixture that has been designed as a useful product, with each component present in a measured quantity, e.g. paint, alloy or medicine.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column2:
Bubble the gas through limewater; it turns milky or cloudy.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: How do you test for chlorine gas?
column2:
Damp litmus paper is bleached white.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: State the flame test colours for lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper.
column2:
Lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: What colour precipitate does iron(III) form with sodium hydroxide?
column2:
Brown.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: What colour precipitate does iron(II) form with sodium hydroxide?
column2:
Green.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: How do you test for a sulfate ion?
column2:
Add dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride solution; a white precipitate forms.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: How do you test for a halide ion?
column2:
Add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution: chloride gives white, bromide cream, iodide yellow precipitate.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: Give three advantages of instrumental methods of analysis.
column2:
They are more accurate, more sensitive and faster than chemical tests, and can work on very small samples.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: Why must the chromatography baseline be drawn in pencil?
column2:
Pencil graphite is insoluble in the solvent, so it will not travel up the paper and interfere with the results.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: How does melting point indicate purity?
column2:
A pure substance melts at one specific temperature; a mixture melts over a range of temperatures.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C8 Chemical Analysis
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C8_Chemical_Analysis AQA::8462 Basic

column1: What are the four stages of a life cycle assessment?
column2:
Extracting and processing raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use and operation during lifetime, and disposal at end of life including transport at every stage.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C10 Using Resources
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C10_Using_Resources AQA::8462 Basic

column1: What is potable water?
column2:
Water that is safe to drink - it has low levels of dissolved salts and microbes, but is not chemically pure.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C10 Using Resources
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C10_Using_Resources AQA::8462 Basic

column1: Describe UK treatment of fresh water to make it potable.
column2:
Pass through filter beds of wire mesh and sand to remove solids, then sterilise with chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462 · C10 Using Resources
column3: GCSE Year11 Chemistry_Triple Chemistry_Triple::C10_Using_Resources AQA::8462 Basic

column1: Why is desalination expensive?
column2:
Distillation or reverse osmosis both require large amounts of energy.

Plants absorb metal compounds from low-grade ore; the plants are burned and the ash, which contains a high concentration of the metal compound, is processed to extract the metal.

Bacteria are used to produce leachate solutions containing metal compounds, from which the metal can be extracted by displacement or electrolysis.

Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

Industrially in several integrated stages on a large continuous scale; in the lab by a single-batch titration of ammonia solution with dilute sulfuric acid followed by crystallisation.

If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the position of equilibrium shifts to counteract that change.

Particles have more kinetic energy so they collide more frequently, and a greater proportion of collisions have energy above the activation energy.

It reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction.

That the core contains magnetic material and that the field is generated within the Earth.

When the wire is parallel to the magnetic field lines.

Potential difference across the primary over potential difference across the secondary equals number of primary turns over number of secondary turns.

An alternator uses slip rings and generates alternating current; a dynamo uses a split-ring commutator and generates direct current.

Move the conductor or coil faster, use a stronger magnetic field, or increase the number of turns on the coil.

A changing magnetic field is needed in the iron core to induce a potential difference in the secondary coil; direct current gives a constant field and no induction.

Pressure variations in sound waves move a diaphragm attached to a coil in a magnetic field, inducing a varying current that represents the sound.

Atom about 1 times 10 to the minus 10 metres; nucleus about 1 times 10 to the minus 14 metres, roughly one ten-thousandth of the atom.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463 · P4 Atomic Structure and Radioactivity

column2:
That the mass of an atom is concentrated in a tiny positively charged nucleus with mostly empty space around it, replacing the plum pudding model.

column2:
Alpha is stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air; beta is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium; gamma is only partly absorbed by thick lead or concrete.

column2:
Alpha, because of its large mass and 2 plus charge - but it has the shortest range.

column2:
The time taken for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve, or for the activity or count rate to halve.

column2:
A neutron becomes a proton and a high-speed electron is emitted, so the mass number stays the same and the atomic number increases by 1.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463 · P4 Atomic Structure and Radioactivity

column1: What changes in the nucleus during alpha decay?
column2:
The nucleus emits two protons and two neutrons, so the mass number decreases by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463 · P4 Atomic Structure and Radioactivity

column2:
Contamination is unwanted radioactive atoms being present on or in an object; irradiation is exposing an object to radiation without it becoming radioactive.

column2:
Neither changes - gamma emission only removes energy from the nucleus.

column2:
Independent checking of published findings ensures conclusions are valid before the public and policymakers rely on them.

column2:
The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, usually after it absorbs a neutron, releasing energy plus two or three neutrons and gamma rays.

column2:
Neutrons released by one fission event go on to cause further fission events, so the reaction sustains itself.

column2:
They absorb neutrons so the rate of fission can be controlled and kept steady.

column2:
Two light nuclei joining to form a heavier nucleus, with some of the mass converted into energy released as radiation.

column2:
Both nuclei are positively charged and repel each other, so enormous energy is needed to bring them close enough for fusion to occur.

Fission produces radioactive waste that needs long-term storage; fusion produces helium, with far less radioactive waste.

The outward pressure from energy released by fusion balances the inward force of gravity.

It expands to a red giant, then the core contracts, shedding its outer layers to leave a white dwarf that cools.

It becomes a red supergiant, then explodes as a supernova, leaving either a neutron star or, if massive enough, a black hole.

They are produced in a supernova explosion, which also distributes the elements through the universe.

Its direction is constantly changing, so its velocity changes; gravity provides the centripetal force causing this acceleration.

Light from receding galaxies has its wavelength increased towards the red end of the spectrum; the greater the red-shift, the faster the galaxy is moving away, which supports an expanding universe.

A greater orbital speed is required for a stable orbit at a smaller radius.

A cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity, heating up as it contracts until fusion begins.

The energy supplied is used to break the bonds between particles rather than to increase their kinetic energy.

Density equals mass divided by volume.

Pressure equals height of the column times density of the liquid times gravitational field strength.

Particles move randomly and collide with the container walls, each collision exerting a force; pressure is the total force per unit area.

Pressure increases, because the particles move faster and collide with the walls more often and more forcefully.

There are fewer air molecules above, so the weight of air acting on a given area is lower, and the atmosphere is also less dense at higher altitude.

Upthrust is the upward force from a fluid due to the pressure difference between the bottom and top of an object; it floats when upthrust equals its weight.

Work done transfers energy to the internal energy store of the gas, so its temperature increases.

Work done equals force times distance moved along the line of action of the force.

Power equals energy transferred divided by time.

Power equals current squared times resistance.

Speed.

The Hadley cell, the Ferrel cell and the Polar cell.

Sea surface temperature above about 27 degrees Celsius, ocean depth of at least 60 to 70 metres, latitude between 5 and 30 degrees for the Coriolis effect, and low wind shear.

The Saffir-Simpson scale, from category 1 to category 5, based on sustained wind speed.

Calm, clear, descending air with the lowest pressure and no rain, surrounded by the most violent conditions in the eye wall.

column2:
A rise in sea level caused by low pressure and strong onshore winds; it causes rapid coastal flooding and is often the biggest cause of death.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 1a Hazardous Earth: Climate and Tropical Cyclones

Ice cores, tree rings (dendrochronology), historical records, sea level change and glacial retreat.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 1a Hazardous Earth: Climate and Tropical Cyclones

column2:
Orbital or Milankovitch cycles, volcanic eruptions releasing ash and aerosols, variations in solar output, and asteroid impacts.

column2:
Weaker building standards, poorer warning and evacuation systems, less money for defences, and greater dependence on agriculture for income.

Convection currents in the mantle, ridge push at constructive boundaries, and slab pull at destructive boundaries.

The denser oceanic plate subducts beneath the continental plate, causing deep earthquakes, explosive volcanoes and fold mountains.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 1b Hazardous Earth: Tectonic Hazards

column1: What happens at a divergent boundary?
column2:
Plates move apart, magma rises to form new crust, producing shallow earthquakes and gentle volcanic activity, e.g. mid-ocean ridges.

When violent ground shaking causes saturated loose soil to behave like a liquid, so buildings sink or tilt.

Fertile volcanic soils, geothermal energy, tourism, mineral resources, family and cultural ties, and a belief that the risk is low or manageable.

column2:
Cross-bracing and shock absorbers or base isolators, deep foundations into bedrock, and lightweight roofing materials.

Two continental plates of similar density collide with no subduction, so crust buckles into fold mountains and there are earthquakes but no volcanoes.

Life expectancy at birth, education (mean and expected years of schooling), and GNI per capita.

It is a mean, so it hides inequality, ignores the informal economy, and says nothing about health, education or quality of life.

column2:
Countries move through five stages - traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity, and age of mass consumption - as investment and industry grow.

column1: Summarise Franks dependency theory.
column2:
Poorer countries remain poor because a core of wealthy nations extracts resources and value from a periphery, keeping it dependent.

column2:
Advantages: employment and higher wages, transfer of skills and technology, multiplier effect. Disadvantages: profits leave the country, poor working conditions, environmental damage, and vulnerability if the TNC relocates.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 2 Development Dynamics (India case study)

column1: What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up development?
column2:
Top-down is large scale, government or TNC-led and expensive, e.g. a dam; bottom-up is small scale, community-led and locally appropriate, e.g. a village water pump.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 2 Development Dynamics (India case study)

column1: What is the multiplier effect?
column2:
Initial investment creates jobs and income, which is spent locally, creating further demand, jobs and tax revenue in a self-reinforcing cycle.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 2 Development Dynamics (India case study)

column1: Define urbanisation.
column2:
The increase in the proportion of a countrys population living in urban areas.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 3 Challenges of an Urbanising World (Mumbai case study)

column2:
A city with a population of more than 10 million people.

column2:
Push: lack of jobs, poor services, mechanisation of farming, drought or conflict. Pull: better paid work, education, healthcare, and perceived higher quality of life.
