column1: Why did Mumbai grow so rapidly?
column2:
A deep natural harbour and colonial port trade, then textile industry, Bollywood and financial services, plus continuing rural-urban migration and natural increase.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 3 Challenges of an Urbanising World (Mumbai case study)

column1: Give two opportunities and two challenges of life in Dharavi.
column2:
Opportunities: a large informal economy with recycling and small manufacturing, strong community networks. Challenges: extreme population density, inadequate sanitation and clean water, and insecure tenure.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 3 Challenges of an Urbanising World (Mumbai case study)

column1: What was Vision Mumbai?
column2:
A top-down redevelopment plan to improve Mumbai by replacing slums with high-rise housing and upgrading transport, sanitation and the economy.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 3 Challenges of an Urbanising World (Mumbai case study)

column1: Why can top-down slum clearance be unpopular with residents?
column2:
It can break up communities and informal businesses, replacement housing may be unaffordable or badly located, and residents are rarely consulted.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 3 Challenges of an Urbanising World (Mumbai case study)

column1: Define stratified sampling in fieldwork.
column2:
Dividing the study area or population into subgroups and sampling each in proportion to its size, so all groups are represented.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 6 Geographical Investigations (Human and Physical Fieldwork)

column1: Why is systematic sampling used along a river or transect?
column2:
It gives evenly spaced measurements, which makes it easy to show change with distance and to replicate.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 6 Geographical Investigations (Human and Physical Fieldwork)

column1: Give two limitations of using questionnaires in an urban quality of life enquiry.
column2:
Responses are subjective and may be biased, and the sample may not be representative if it is collected at one time of day or place.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 6 Geographical Investigations (Human and Physical Fieldwork)

column1: What is a choropleth map best used for?
column2:
Showing how a quantity varies between defined areas using graded shading, e.g. population density by ward.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 6 Geographical Investigations (Human and Physical Fieldwork)

column1: Why must a risk assessment be completed before fieldwork?
column2:
To identify hazards such as traffic, deep or fast-flowing water, and weather, and to plan measures that reduce the likelihood or severity of harm.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 6 Geographical Investigations (Human and Physical Fieldwork)

column1: What is the difference between reliability and accuracy in fieldwork data?
column2:
Reliability is whether repeating the method gives consistent results; accuracy is how close the measurement is to the true value.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 6 Geographical Investigations (Human and Physical Fieldwork)

column1: How do you give a six-figure grid reference?
column2:
Eastings first then northings; read the two-digit gridline then estimate tenths across the square, for both axes.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Topic 6 Geographical Investigations (Human and Physical Fieldwork)

column1: What two climatic factors most strongly control global biome distribution?
column2:
Temperature and precipitation, which are largely determined by latitude and global atmospheric circulation.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Paper 3 People and Environment Issues (Topics 7, 8 and 9)

column1: Why are rainforest soils infertile despite dense vegetation?
column2:
Nutrients are stored in the biomass, not the soil; rapid decomposition and heavy leaching mean nutrients are taken up immediately or washed away.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Paper 3 People and Environment Issues (Topics 7, 8 and 9)

column1: Give four causes of tropical deforestation.
column2:
Commercial logging, cattle ranching and soy or palm oil plantations, mineral extraction, hydroelectric and road development, and subsistence farming or settlement.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Paper 3 People and Environment Issues (Topics 7, 8 and 9)

column1: Why does the taiga have low biodiversity?
column2:
Long cold winters, a short growing season, acidic nutrient-poor podsol soils and limited water availability when frozen restrict the range of species.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Paper 3 People and Environment Issues (Topics 7, 8 and 9)

column1: What is selective logging and why is it more sustainable?
column2:
Only mature or lower-value trees are felled, leaving the canopy and younger trees intact so the forest regenerates and habitat is retained.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Paper 3 People and Environment Issues (Topics 7, 8 and 9)

column1: Define energy security.
column2:
Uninterrupted access to sufficient, affordable and reliable energy supplies to meet a countrys needs.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Paper 3 People and Environment Issues (Topics 7, 8 and 9)

column1: Give two environmental costs of extracting oil from tar sands.
column2:
Large-scale removal of boreal forest and soil, high water use and toxic tailings ponds, and high carbon emissions per barrel produced.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Paper 3 People and Environment Issues (Topics 7, 8 and 9)

column1: What does the Paper 3 12-mark decision-making question require?
column2:
Use the resource booklet to weigh the given options against stated criteria such as cost, environment and people, choose one, justify it with evidence, and acknowledge its drawbacks and the rejected options.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Paper 3 People and Environment Issues (Topics 7, 8 and 9)

column1: What is net primary productivity?
column2:
The rate at which plants store energy as biomass after their own respiration, usually measured in grams per square metre per year.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Paper 3 People and Environment Issues (Topics 7, 8 and 9)

column1: Name the four coastal erosion processes.
column2:
Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Retrieval: UK Physical and Evolving Human Landscapes (Topics 4 and 5)

column1: Describe the sequence forming a stack.
column2:
A crack in a headland is widened by erosion into a cave, the cave erodes through to form an arch, the arch roof collapses leaving a stack, which is undercut to leave a stump.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Retrieval: UK Physical and Evolving Human Landscapes (Topics 4 and 5)

column1: What is longshore drift?
column2:
The zigzag movement of sediment along a coast caused by waves approaching at an angle, with swash moving material diagonally up the beach and backwash returning it straight down.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Retrieval: UK Physical and Evolving Human Landscapes (Topics 4 and 5)

column1: Compare hard and soft engineering.
column2:
Hard engineering uses built structures such as sea walls and groynes - effective but expensive and often visually intrusive. Soft engineering works with natural processes, e.g. beach nourishment or managed retreat - cheaper and more sustainable but less immediately protective.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Retrieval: UK Physical and Evolving Human Landscapes (Topics 4 and 5)

column1: How does an ox-bow lake form?
column2:
Erosion on the outside bends narrows the meander neck until a flood cuts through; deposition then seals off the old meander, leaving a curved lake.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Retrieval: UK Physical and Evolving Human Landscapes (Topics 4 and 5)

column1: What does lag time on a hydrograph mean, and what shortens it?
column2:
The time between peak rainfall and peak discharge. Impermeable rock, steep slopes, urbanisation, saturated or frozen ground and deforestation all shorten it, increasing flood risk.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Retrieval: UK Physical and Evolving Human Landscapes (Topics 4 and 5)

column1: What is deindustrialisation and how did it affect Birmingham?
column2:
The decline of manufacturing employment. In Birmingham it caused job losses in car and metal industries, unemployment and derelict land, later addressed by service-sector growth and city-centre regeneration.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Retrieval: UK Physical and Evolving Human Landscapes (Topics 4 and 5)

column1: What is rural rebranding?
column2:
Changing the image and function of a rural area, often through tourism, heritage or specialist food production, to attract visitors and investment.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0 · Retrieval: UK Physical and Evolving Human Landscapes (Topics 4 and 5)

column1: When do you use the preterite rather than the imperfect in Spanish?
column2:
The preterite describes completed single actions in the past; the imperfect describes ongoing, repeated or background situations.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 1 Identity and Culture: Customs and Traditions

column1: Give the first person preterite of celebrar.
column2:
Celebré - I celebrated. Note the written accent on the final e; without it, celebre is the subjunctive.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 1 Identity and Culture: Customs and Traditions

column1: How do you say in my opinion in Spanish, at higher level?
column2:
En mi opinión, or a mi parecer, or desde mi punto de vista.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 1 Identity and Culture: Customs and Traditions

column1: How do you form the superlative in Spanish?
column2:
Definite article plus más or menos plus adjective, e.g. la fiesta más importante.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 1 Identity and Culture: Customs and Traditions

column1: Give three linking words that raise your writing grade.
column2:
Sin embargo (however), aunque (although), por lo tanto (therefore), ya que (since).

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 1 Identity and Culture: Customs and Traditions

column1: How do you form the near future tense in Spanish?
column2:
Ir conjugated plus a plus the infinitive, e.g. voy a estudiar - I am going to study.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 4 Future Aspirations, Study and Work

column1: How do you form the simple future of regular verbs?
column2:
Add é, ás, á, emos, éis, án to the infinitive, e.g. estudiaré - I will study.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 4 Future Aspirations, Study and Work

column1: How do you form the conditional?
column2:
Add ía, ías, ía, íamos, íais, ían to the infinitive, e.g. me gustaría - I would like.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 4 Future Aspirations, Study and Work

column1: Which mood follows cuando when talking about the future?
column2:
The present subjunctive, e.g. cuando termine mis estudios - when I finish my studies.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 4 Future Aspirations, Study and Work

column1: Translate: I would like to work abroad because I want to improve my Spanish.
column2:
Me gustaría trabajar en el extranjero porque quiero mejorar mi español.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 4 Future Aspirations, Study and Work

column1: How do you say we should recycle more in Spanish?
column2:
Deberíamos reciclar más.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 5 International and Global Dimension

column1: What does hay que plus infinitive express?
column2:
An impersonal obligation - one must, it is necessary to.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 5 International and Global Dimension

column1: Give three environmental problems in Spanish.
column2:
La contaminación (pollution), el calentamiento global (global warming), la deforestación (deforestation), la sequía (drought).

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 5 International and Global Dimension

column1: What is the impersonal se used for?
column2:
To say something is done in general without naming who does it, e.g. se recicla el plástico - plastic is recycled.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 5 International and Global Dimension

column1: How many words should a higher-tier extended writing answer be?
column2:
Around 130 to 150 words, using at least two tenses and developed opinions.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Theme 5 International and Global Dimension

column1: Explain the difference between ser and estar.
column2:
Ser is for permanent or defining characteristics, origin, profession and time. Estar is for temporary states, moods and location.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Grammar Core and Exam Technique
column3: GCSE Year11 Spanish Spanish::Grammar_Core_and_Exam_Technique Pearson::1SP1 Basic

column1: When do you use por and when para?
column2:
Por for cause, exchange, duration and movement through. Para for purpose, destination, deadline and recipient.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Grammar Core and Exam Technique
column3: GCSE Year11 Spanish Spanish::Grammar_Core_and_Exam_Technique Pearson::1SP1 Basic

column1: Where do object pronouns usually go in Spanish?
column2:
Before the conjugated verb, or attached to the end of an infinitive, gerund or positive command.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Grammar Core and Exam Technique
column3: GCSE Year11 Spanish Spanish::Grammar_Core_and_Exam_Technique Pearson::1SP1 Basic

column1: Name three tenses that will lift a higher-tier written answer.
column2:
The preterite, the conditional and the subjunctive, alongside the present and near future.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Grammar Core and Exam Technique
column3: GCSE Year11 Spanish Spanish::Grammar_Core_and_Exam_Technique Pearson::1SP1 Basic

column1: Give a fast listening exam strategy.
column2:
Read the questions before the recording, predict likely vocabulary, and listen actively for numbers, negatives and time markers on the first play.

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Grammar Core and Exam Technique
column3: GCSE Year11 Spanish Spanish::Grammar_Core_and_Exam_Technique Pearson::1SP1 Basic

column1: Which five words change meaning only because of a written accent?
column2:
sí (yes) versus si (if), él (he) versus el (the), tú (you) versus tu (your), más (more) versus mas (but), sólo/solo and qué (what, in questions) versus que (that).

Spanish · Pearson Edexcel 1SP1 · Grammar Core and Exam Technique
column3: GCSE Year11 Spanish Spanish::Grammar_Core_and_Exam_Technique Pearson::1SP1 Basic

column1: What are the three omni-attributes of God in Christianity?
column2:
Omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing) and omnibenevolent (all-loving).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What is the Trinity?
column2:
The belief that God exists as three persons - Father, Son and Holy Spirit - who are three distinct persons but one God.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What does the incarnation mean?
column2:
The belief that God became human in the person of Jesus Christ, who is fully God and fully human.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What is original sin?
column2:
The belief that all humans inherit a sinful nature from the disobedience of Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What does the crucifixion achieve for Christians?
column2:
It is an act of atonement - Jesus dies to pay the price for human sin and restore the relationship between God and humanity.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: Give a Bible quotation showing God's omnipotence.
column2:
"For nothing is impossible with God" (Luke 1:37).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: Give a Bible quotation about the Trinity or Jesus' baptism.
column2:
At Jesus' baptism: "You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased" (Mark 1:11), showing Father, Son and Spirit together.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What does John 3:16 teach about salvation?
column2:
"For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life."

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: How do Christians explain the problem of evil and suffering?
column2:
Some say suffering is a test of faith, some say it results from free will and human sin, and some say God allows it for a greater good or to develop character.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What is the difference between a literalist and a liberal Christian view of Genesis?
column2:
Literalists believe Genesis is a factual, historical account of creation; liberal Christians see it as a symbolic or metaphorical account compatible with evolution and the Big Bang.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What happens at judgement, according to Christian belief?
column2:
After death, souls are judged by God according to their faith and actions; the righteous go to heaven and the unrighteous to hell.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: Why is the resurrection important for Christians?
column2:
It shows Jesus conquered death, confirms his divinity, and gives Christians hope of eternal life after death.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What is the difference between liturgical and non-liturgical worship?
column2:
Liturgical worship follows a fixed structure or set order of service, such as Holy Communion; non-liturgical worship is more informal, with spontaneous prayer and preaching.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What is the Lord's Prayer and why is it important?
column2:
The set prayer taught by Jesus to his disciples (Matthew 6:9-13), used by almost all Christian denominations as a model for how to pray.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What is the difference between infant baptism and believers' baptism?
column2:
Infant baptism is performed on babies as a sign of the family's faith and welcome into the church; believers' baptism is a conscious adult choice, usually by full immersion, after a person can understand and declare their own faith.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What do Catholics believe happens during Holy Communion?
column2:
Transubstantiation - the bread and wine actually become the body and blood of Christ while keeping their outward appearance.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What do most Protestants believe Holy Communion represents?
column2:
A memorial or symbolic act that remembers Jesus' sacrifice at the Last Supper, rather than a literal change in the bread and wine.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: Give a Bible quotation associated with the Last Supper or Holy Communion.
column2:
"This is my body given for you; do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: Why do Christians go on pilgrimage to Lourdes?
column2:
Lourdes is associated with reported miracles and apparitions of the Virgin Mary to Saint Bernadette, and pilgrims go seeking healing, to grow in faith, or to support others who are sick.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: Give two ways churches help their local community.
column2:
Running food banks for those in poverty, and street pastors who support vulnerable people on Friday and Saturday nights in town centres.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What is the Great Commission?
column2:
Jesus' final instruction to his disciples to go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them (Matthew 28:19), which underpins Christian mission and evangelism.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What is the difference between mission and evangelism?
column2:
Mission is the broader work of spreading the gospel and serving communities, often including practical aid; evangelism specifically means preaching the gospel to convert people to Christianity.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: How do churches respond to the persecution of Christians worldwide?
column2:
Through prayer, raising awareness, campaigning for religious freedom, and financially supporting persecuted Christians through organisations such as Open Doors.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What does Agape mean and why does it matter in Christian practice?
column2:
Agape is selfless, unconditional love; it motivates Christian charity, forgiveness and service to others regardless of whether it is returned.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Christianity Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Christianity_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What were the Four Sights the Buddha encountered?
column2:
An old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a holy man (ascetic) - they showed him that suffering, old age and death are unavoidable, and that a holy life could offer a way beyond suffering.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What happened during the Buddha's Enlightenment?
column2:
Sitting under the Bodhi tree, he resisted the temptations of Mara over three watches of the night and gained insight into the Four Noble Truths, becoming enlightened.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: State the Three Marks of Existence.
column2:
Anicca (impermanence), anatta (no fixed or permanent self), and dukkha (suffering).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: State the Four Noble Truths.
column2:
1) Suffering (dukkha) exists. 2) Suffering is caused by craving (tanha). 3) Suffering can end. 4) The Eightfold Path is the way to end suffering.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: Give two of the Three Poisons.
column2:
Greed (attachment) and hatred (aversion) - the third is ignorance (delusion).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What is dependent arising (paticcasamuppada)?
column2:
The teaching that nothing exists independently - everything arises because of causes and conditions, and ceases when those conditions cease.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What are the Five Aggregates in Theravada Buddhism?
column2:
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations and consciousness - the five changing components that make up what is mistakenly seen as a permanent self.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What is the difference between an Arhat and a Bodhisattva?
column2:
An Arhat (Theravada ideal) is someone who has followed the Eightfold Path and reached enlightenment for themselves; a Bodhisattva (Mahayana ideal) delays their own final Nirvana to help all other beings reach enlightenment first.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What is sunyata in Mahayana Buddhism?
column2:
Emptiness - the teaching that all things lack a fixed, independent existence and are empty of a permanent self, linked to anatta.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: Who is Amitabha Buddha and what is Sukhavati?
column2:
Amitabha is a Buddha revered in Pure Land Buddhism; Sukhavati is his Pure Land, a place where rebirth allows easier progress toward enlightenment.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What is samsara?
column2:
The continuous cycle of birth, death and rebirth, driven by karma, from which Buddhists seek liberation through reaching Nirvana.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: Give a quotation from the Dhammapada about the mind or suffering.
column2:
"All that we are is the result of what we have thought" (Dhammapada 1:1), showing the mind's role in shaping experience and suffering.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Beliefs and Teachings

column1: What is a vihara?
column2:
A Buddhist monastery, where monks and nuns live, and often a centre of worship and teaching for lay Buddhists.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What is puja?
column2:
An act of devotional worship, which may include chanting, making offerings such as flowers, candles or incense, and showing respect before a Buddha rupa (statue).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What is the difference between samatha and vipassana meditation?
column2:
Samatha meditation calms and focuses the mind, often through mindfulness of breathing; vipassana (insight) meditation aims to see the true nature of reality, including impermanence and no-self.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: Why is meditation not "emptying the mind"?
column2:
It is a method of calming and focusing the mind through concentration and awareness, not simply making the mind blank.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What is Wesak and why is it important?
column2:
The most important Buddhist festival, celebrating the Buddha's birth, Enlightenment and death (in Theravada tradition) on one day, with acts of devotion, decorating shrines, and charitable giving.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: State the Five Moral Precepts.
column2:
Avoid harming living things; avoid taking what is not given; avoid sexual misconduct; avoid wrong speech; avoid substances that cloud the mind.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: Name the Four Sublime States (Brahmaviharas).
column2:
Metta (loving-kindness), karuna (compassion), mudita (sympathetic joy) and upekkha (equanimity).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: Give two of the Six Perfections (paramitas).
column2:
Generosity (dana) and patience (khanti) - others are morality, energy, meditation and wisdom.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What is the difference between metta and karuna?
column2:
Metta is loving-kindness, a general goodwill towards all beings; karuna is compassion, the wish to actively relieve the suffering of others.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: Why might Buddhists disagree about whether it is possible to always act with karuna?
column2:
Some argue enlightened beings such as Bodhisattvas show unconditional compassion at all times; others note ordinary Buddhists still experience the Three Poisons and may fail to act compassionately under pressure.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What are skilful and unskilful actions in Buddhism?
column2:
Skilful actions arise from generosity, loving-kindness and wisdom and lead to good karma; unskilful actions arise from greed, hatred and ignorance and lead to bad karma.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What is a mala and how is it used?
column2:
A string of beads used to count mantra recitations or breaths during meditation, helping focus concentration.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Buddhism Practices
column3: GCSE Year11 Religious_Studies Religious_Studies::Buddhism_Practices AQA::8062 Basic

column1: What does Genesis 1 teach about the origin of the universe?
column2:
God created the universe and everything in it over six days, and rested on the seventh, declaring his creation good.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: How might a liberal Christian reconcile Genesis with the Big Bang theory?
column2:
They may see Genesis as a symbolic or theological account of God's role as ultimate creator, compatible with the Big Bang and evolution as the scientific mechanisms God used.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: What is the difference between stewardship and dominion?
column2:
Stewardship is the belief that humans must care for and look after the Earth on God's behalf; dominion is the belief that humans have authority or rule over the Earth and its creatures, given by God.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: Give a Bible quotation relevant to stewardship of the environment.
column2:
"The Lord God took the man and put him in the Garden of Eden to work it and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: What is the Buddhist view on the use of animals?
column2:
Many Buddhists are vegetarian because of the First Precept (avoid harming living things) and the belief in the interconnectedness and value of all sentient life.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: What is the sanctity of life?
column2:
The belief that life is sacred, holy and belongs to God (or is precious and irreplaceable), so it should be respected and protected.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: Give one religious argument against abortion.
column2:
Many Christians argue life begins at conception and is sacred (sanctity of life), citing Jeremiah 1:5, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you."

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: Give one religious argument that could support abortion in some circumstances.
column2:
Some liberal Christians emphasise quality of life and compassion, arguing abortion may be the lesser of two evils, for example to protect the mother's life or health.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: What is euthanasia and what are its two main types?
column2:
Ending a person's life to relieve suffering; voluntary euthanasia (with the person's consent) and non-voluntary or involuntary euthanasia (without consent, e.g. person unable to consent).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: Give a religious argument against euthanasia.
column2:
Many Christians argue only God has the right to give and take life (sanctity of life), and that euthanasia is a form of killing that goes against the Sixth Commandment.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: What do Buddhists generally believe happens after death?
column2:
Rebirth (samsara) according to karma, continuing until a person reaches Nirvana and is liberated from the cycle of rebirth.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: Give two reasons religious believers might oppose animal experimentation.
column2:
It may cause unnecessary suffering to sentient creatures, and some believe humans do not have the right to exploit animals purely for human benefit.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme B: Religion and Life

column1: State the main criteria of Just War theory.
column2:
The war must have a just cause; be declared by a proper authority; have a reasonable chance of success; be a last resort; the response must be proportionate; and it must aim to bring about peace.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: What is Holy War?
column2:
A war believed to be commanded, sanctioned or blessed by God, fought for a religious cause.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: What is pacifism?
column2:
The belief that violence and war can never be justified, and that peaceful means should always be used to resolve conflict.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: Give a Bible quotation relevant to pacifism.
column2:
"You have heard that it was said, 'Eye for eye'... But I tell you, turn the other cheek" (Matthew 5:38-39).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: Give a Bible quotation about peace or peacemakers.
column2:
"Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God" (Matthew 5:9).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: What is the Buddhist First Precept and how does it relate to war?
column2:
The First Precept is to avoid harming living things (ahimsa); many Buddhists see this as a strong basis for pacifism and opposition to war and violence.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: Give two religious concerns about weapons of mass destruction.
column2:
They cause indiscriminate suffering to civilians and combatants alike, and violate the just war principle of proportionality; some argue they threaten the sanctity of all life on a massive scale.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: Give two ways religious believers help victims of war.
column2:
Providing practical aid such as food, shelter and medical care through religious charities, and offering prayer, counselling and support for trauma and reconciliation.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: Why is Coventry Cathedral significant for religion and reconciliation?
column2:
Destroyed by bombing in the Second World War, it became a symbol of reconciliation and forgiveness, including the Community of the Cross of Nails, which promotes peace-building worldwide.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: Give a reason why religion can be a cause of conflict.
column2:
Differences in religious belief or interpretation can lead to intolerance, division between groups, or be used to justify violence, as seen historically in the Northern Ireland Troubles.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: Why might the Northern Ireland Troubles be seen as more political than religious?
column2:
Although the conflict was between mostly Protestant and Catholic communities, many argue the underlying causes were political and social identity and inequality rather than pure religious doctrine.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: What does retaliation mean in the context of reasons for war?
column2:
Responding to an attack or perceived wrong with force, often to deter future aggression or to seek revenge.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme D: Religion, Peace and Conflict

column1: State the four main aims of punishment.
column2:
Retribution (making the criminal suffer for their crime), deterrence (discouraging crime through fear of punishment), reformation (helping the criminal change and improve), and protection of the public.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: Give two reasons people might commit crime, according to religious teaching.
column2:
Poverty and desperation, and mental illness or addiction - other causes include greed, hatred, and upbringing.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: Give a Bible quotation about forgiveness.
column2:
"Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, 'Lord, how many times shall I forgive?'... Jesus answered, 'Not seven times, but seventy-seven times'" (Matthew 18:21-22).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: Why do Christians believe forgiveness is important?
column2:
Jesus taught forgiveness repeatedly and forgave those who wronged him (even on the cross), and Christians believe God forgives them, so they should forgive others in turn.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: Give a religious argument against the death penalty.
column2:
Many Christians argue only God has the right to give and take life (sanctity of life), and that Jesus taught forgiveness and mercy rather than revenge.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: Give a religious argument that could support the death penalty.
column2:
Some cite Old Testament justice such as "eye for eye" (Exodus 21:24) or argue the death penalty protects society and delivers retribution proportionate to the crime.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: What is the Buddhist view of the death penalty?
column2:
Most Buddhists oppose it because it breaks the First Precept against harming living beings and denies the possibility of the criminal changing their karma through reform.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: Who is Gee Walker and why is she used as a case study?
column2:
The mother of Anthony Walker, murdered in a racist attack, who publicly forgave his killers, illustrating Christian teaching on forgiveness in practice.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: How does the Buddhist idea of karma relate to crime?
column2:
Unskilful (unwholesome) actions such as crime create bad karma that will affect future rebirths, so criminals are encouraged to acknowledge wrongdoing and change their behaviour.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: What does corporal punishment mean?
column2:
Punishing a criminal by inflicting physical pain on them, such as caning or whipping.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: Why might reformation be considered the most important aim of punishment by some religious believers?
column2:
Many believe people can change and that a just society should aim to help offenders become law-abiding citizens rather than simply punishing them, reflecting compassion and forgiveness.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme E: Religion, Crime and Punishment

column1: What is the difference between prejudice and discrimination?
column2:
Prejudice is a negative attitude or pre-judgement of a person or group without good reason; discrimination is acting unfairly against someone because of that prejudice.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: What is positive discrimination?
column2:
Favouring a group that has previously suffered discrimination, for example to increase representation of women or minorities, in order to correct historical unfairness.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: Give a Bible quotation used against racism.
column2:
"There is neither Jew nor Gentile... for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: What are two contrasting Christian views on women in church leadership?
column2:
Some denominations (e.g. many Anglican and Protestant churches) ordain women as priests or ministers; others (e.g. the Roman Catholic Church) restrict the priesthood to men, citing tradition and scripture.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: What are two contrasting Christian views on homosexuality?
column2:
Some liberal Christians believe same-sex relationships can be loving and are acceptable to God; others, citing passages such as Leviticus 18:22, believe homosexual acts go against biblical teaching.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: What is a tithe?
column2:
Giving a proportion (traditionally a tenth) of one's income to God or the church, reflecting religious teaching on generosity and stewardship of wealth.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: Give a Bible quotation about wealth and its dangers.
column2:
"It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God" (Matthew 19:24).

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: What is the Buddhist attitude to wealth?
column2:
Wealth itself is not wrong, but attachment (tanha) to wealth and greed are seen as causes of suffering; Buddhists are encouraged to be generous (dana) and not become attached to possessions.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: Give two ways the poor can be exploited.
column2:
Being paid unfairly low wages for their labour, and being trafficked or trapped in forced labour or modern slavery.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: What is the difference between emergency aid and long-term aid?
column2:
Emergency aid provides immediate short-term relief after a crisis, such as food, water and shelter after a disaster; long-term aid works on sustainable development, such as building infrastructure, education or clean water systems, to prevent future poverty.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: Give a religious reason for helping the poor.
column2:
Many Christians cite the parable of the Good Samaritan and Jesus' teaching "whatever you did for one of the least of these... you did for me" (Matthew 25:40) as a duty to help those in need.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: What is human trafficking?
column2:
The illegal transport and exploitation of people, often through force or deception, for labour, sexual exploitation or other forms of modern slavery - widely condemned by religious teaching on human dignity.

Religious Studies · AQA 8062 · Theme F: Religion, Human Rights and Social Justice

column1: What is the main function of protein in the body?
column2:
Growth and repair of body cells and tissues; it can also provide energy in extreme circumstances.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: What is an essential amino acid?
column2:
An amino acid the body cannot make itself, so it must be obtained from food.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: What is a high biological value (HBV) protein?
column2:
A protein containing all the essential amino acids in the right proportions the body needs, usually from animal sources.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: What is protein complementation?
column2:
Combining two or more low biological value protein sources, such as beans and rice, so that together they provide all the essential amino acids.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: Name the two categories of fatty acids and give one health effect of each.
column2:
Saturated fatty acids (mainly animal fats) can raise blood cholesterol and heart disease risk; unsaturated fatty acids (mainly plant and fish oils) can help lower blood cholesterol.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: What is the difference between visible and invisible fat?
column2:
Visible fat can be seen and cut off, such as the fat on meat or butter; invisible fat is hidden within a food, such as in cheese, cakes or nuts.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: What are the three types of carbohydrate?
column2:
Sugars, starches and dietary fibre (non-starch polysaccharide).

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: Give one function of dietary fibre.
column2:
It aids digestion and helps prevent bowel disorders by adding bulk to waste and helping it move through the gut.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: What health problems are linked to excess sugar intake?
column2:
Tooth decay, obesity and increased risk of type 2 diabetes.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: What is kwashiorkor?
column2:
A severe protein deficiency disease causing swollen abdomen, muscle wasting and stunted growth, mainly seen in children with inadequate diets.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: Name two sources of essential fatty acids.
column2:
Oily fish (e.g. salmon, mackerel) and vegetable oils (e.g. sunflower, olive oil).

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: Why do energy needs vary between individuals?
column2:
Energy needs depend on age, gender, body size and physical activity level (PAL); more active people and growing teenagers need more energy.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Macronutrients

column1: Name the four fat soluble vitamins.
column2:
Vitamins A, D, E and K.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: What condition results from vitamin D deficiency in children?
column2:
Rickets, causing soft, weak bones that can bow or bend.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: What is the main function of vitamin C?
column2:
Antioxidant, helps the immune system, aids iron absorption, and is needed for healthy skin and connective tissue (collagen).

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: What deficiency disease is caused by lack of vitamin C?
column2:
Scurvy, causing bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: What is the main function of calcium?
column2:
Builds and maintains strong bones and teeth, and helps blood clot and muscles function.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: What is the main function of iron?
column2:
Makes haemoglobin in red blood cells, which carries oxygen around the body.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: What condition results from iron deficiency?
column2:
Iron deficiency anaemia, causing tiredness, pale skin and breathlessness.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: Why should sodium intake be limited?
column2:
Excess sodium (salt) is linked to high blood pressure and increased risk of stroke and heart disease.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: What are the nutritional priorities for a toddler compared to an adult?
column2:
Toddlers need energy-dense, nutrient-dense foods in small frequent meals because they have small stomachs but high energy and growth needs relative to size.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: Why do pregnant women need extra folic acid?
column2:
Folic acid reduces the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida in the developing baby.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: What must a coeliac avoid and why?
column2:
Gluten, a protein found in wheat, barley and rye, because it damages the lining of their small intestine.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: Give two effects of dehydration on the body.
column2:
Headaches and reduced concentration; in severe cases dizziness, confusion and, if untreated, organ damage.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food, Nutrition and Health: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Needs

column1: Give three reasons why food is cooked.
column2:
To make it safe to eat by killing bacteria, to improve palatability and digestibility, and to develop flavour, colour and texture.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Cooking and Heat Transfer

column1: Define conduction as a method of heat transfer.
column2:
Heat travels through direct contact between particles, for example heat passing from a hob through the base of a saucepan into food.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Cooking and Heat Transfer

column1: Define convection as a method of heat transfer.
column2:
Heat travels through the movement of currents in a liquid or air, for example hot air circulating in an oven or boiling water circulating heat in a pan.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Cooking and Heat Transfer

column1: Define radiation as a method of heat transfer.
column2:
Heat travels as electromagnetic waves directly onto the food without a medium, for example under a grill or in a toaster.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Cooking and Heat Transfer

column1: How does surface area affect the rate of heat transfer?
column2:
A larger surface area increases the rate of heat transfer, so smaller or thinner pieces of food cook faster.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Cooking and Heat Transfer

column1: Give two dry heat cooking methods.
column2:
Baking and roasting (also grilling and barbecuing).

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Cooking and Heat Transfer

column1: Give two moist heat cooking methods.
column2:
Boiling and steaming (also poaching, stewing and braising).

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Cooking and Heat Transfer

column1: How does a microwave oven heat food?
column2:
Microwaves cause water molecules in the food to vibrate rapidly, generating heat through friction from within the food.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Cooking and Heat Transfer

column1: Why might density and viscosity affect cooking time?
column2:
Denser or more viscous foods transfer heat more slowly, so they take longer to cook through than thin, less dense foods.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Cooking and Heat Transfer

column1: What is the difference between shallow frying and deep frying?
column2:
Shallow frying uses a small amount of fat and cooks the food mainly by conduction from the pan; deep frying submerges food fully in hot fat, cooking it faster on all sides.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Cooking and Heat Transfer

column1: Define denaturation.
column2:
A permanent change to the structure of a protein caused by heat, acid or mechanical action, which changes its shape and properties.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: Give a food example of coagulation.
column2:
Egg white turning from a runny liquid into a solid white when heated, as in a fried or boiled egg.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: What is gelatinisation and give an example?
column2:
Starch granules absorbing liquid and swelling when heated, thickening the mixture, as in a roux-based sauce.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: What is dextrinisation and give an example?
column2:
Dry heat breaking down starch on the surface of food into dextrins, causing browning, as in toasted bread.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: What is caramelisation and give an example?
column2:
Sugar breaking down under heat to form a brown colour and nutty flavour, as in caramel sauce or roasted onions.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: What is emulsification and give an example?
column2:
Combining two liquids that would normally separate, such as oil and water, using an emulsifier like egg yolk lecithin, as in mayonnaise.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: What is plasticity in fats and give an example?
column2:
The ability of a fat to be spread or moulded at room temperature, allowing it to be creamed with sugar, as in butter for a cake mixture.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: What is shortening and give an example?
column2:
Fat coating flour particles to prevent long gluten strands forming, giving a short, crumbly texture, as in shortcrust pastry.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: Name the three types of raising agent.
column2:
Biological (yeast), chemical (baking powder or bicarbonate of soda), and mechanical/physical (whisking, steam or sieving air into flour).

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: Give a food example of aeration by whisking.
column2:
Whisked egg white trapping air to form a foam, as used in meringue.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: How does kneading affect bread dough?
column2:
Kneading develops the gluten network, making the dough elastic and able to trap gas produced by yeast, giving bread its structure.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Science: Functional and Chemical Properties

column1: Name three conditions bacteria need to grow.
column2:
Warmth, moisture and food (nutrients); time is also needed for them to multiply.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: What is the temperature danger zone?
column2:
5 degrees Celsius to 63 degrees Celsius, the range in which food poisoning bacteria multiply fastest.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: Give three examples of high-risk foods.
column2:
Cooked meat and poultry, dairy products, and cooked rice (also eggs, fish and shellfish).

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: What is cross-contamination?
column2:
The transfer of harmful bacteria from one food, surface or piece of equipment to another, e.g. raw meat juices touching ready-to-eat food.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: What are common sources of Salmonella?
column2:
Raw eggs and poultry; symptoms include diarrhoea, vomiting and stomach pain.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: What are common sources of E. coli?
column2:
Raw or undercooked meat and unwashed vegetables; it can cause severe diarrhoea and can survive fridge and freezer temperatures.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: Give an example of physical, chemical and biological contamination.
column2:
Physical: a hair or piece of glass in food. Chemical: cleaning fluid residue on equipment. Biological: bacteria, viruses or moulds.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: What is the difference between a use-by date and a best-before date?
column2:
A use-by date is a safety date - food should not be eaten after this date; a best-before date is a quality date - food may be safely eaten after but quality may decline.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: What core temperature should high-risk food reach when cooked or reheated?
column2:
75 degrees Celsius (held for at least 30 seconds), checked with a temperature probe.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: Give one beneficial use of micro-organisms in food production.
column2:
Yeast ferments sugars to produce carbon dioxide, which raises bread dough.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: How should raw and cooked meat be stored to prevent cross-contamination?
column2:
Raw meat should be stored below and separately from cooked or ready-to-eat foods, ideally on a designated colour-coded board and in a sealed container.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Safety: Spoilage, Contamination and Preparation

column1: Give three factors that can influence food choice.
column2:
Cost, availability of ingredients, and time available to prepare food (also culture, religion, health and personal preference).

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: Give an example of a religious food choice rule.
column2:
Halal meat for Muslims must be slaughtered according to Islamic law; kosher food for Jewish people follows dietary laws such as not mixing meat and dairy.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: Define cuisine.
column2:
A style of cooking characteristic of a particular country or region, using distinctive ingredients, preparation methods and presentation techniques.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: Name the senses used in sensory evaluation of food.
column2:
Sight, smell, taste, touch and sound.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: What is a triangle test in sensory evaluation?
column2:
Tasters are given three samples, two identical and one different, and must identify the odd one out to test if a difference can be detected.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: What is a preference test?
column2:
Tasters state which of two or more samples they prefer, used to find out which product people like best.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: Why must samples be coded in a sensory test?
column2:
To remove bias, so tasters judge the food itself rather than being influenced by knowing the brand or source.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: Name three pieces of mandatory information required on a food label.
column2:
Name of the food, list of ingredients in descending order of weight, and allergen information (also weight, use-by/best-before date and storage instructions).

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: What is the purpose of traffic light labelling?
column2:
To let consumers quickly compare the fat, saturated fat, sugar and salt content of foods using red, amber and green colour coding.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: Why must allergens be highlighted on food labels?
column2:
To protect consumers with allergies or intolerances from accidentally eating an ingredient that could cause a serious or life-threatening reaction.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: Give one way marketing can influence food choice.
column2:
Attractive packaging design or health claims on the front of pack can persuade a consumer to choose one product over another.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Choice: Factors, Labelling, Sensory Testing and Cuisines

column1: Give an example each of a grown, reared and caught food.
column2:
Grown: wheat or potatoes. Reared: beef cattle or chickens. Caught: cod or other wild fish.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Provenance: Growing, Rearing, Processing, Sustainability and Security

column1: Define primary processing and give an example.
column2:
Converting a raw ingredient into an edible food or an ingredient for further use, e.g. milling wheat into flour or pasteurising raw milk.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Provenance: Growing, Rearing, Processing, Sustainability and Security

column1: Define secondary processing and give an example.
column2:
Converting a primary processed food into a new product, e.g. turning flour into bread, or milk into cheese or yoghurt.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Provenance: Growing, Rearing, Processing, Sustainability and Security

column1: What is food fortification and give an example?
column2:
Adding nutrients to food that were lost in processing or were never present, e.g. UK white flour is fortified by law with calcium, iron and B vitamins.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585 · Food Provenance: Growing, Rearing, Processing, Sustainability and Security

column1: Give one argument for and one argument against genetically modified (GM) crops.
column2:
For: GM crops can be bred to resist disease and increase yield, helping food security. Against: there are concerns about long-term health effects and impact on biodiversity.

A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being changed or used up itself.

Gene

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Phenotype

The physical or observable characteristics of an organism, resulting from genotype and environment.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Natural selection
Biology (Triple) · Key definitions across the spec
column2:
The process by which organisms with characteristics best suited to their environment are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.

Species

Ecosystem

Biodiversity

Pathogen

Vaccine

A small, safe dose of dead or inactive pathogen (or its antigens) that stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies, giving immunity without causing disease.

Antibiotic

A medicine that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria without harming human cells; ineffective against viruses.

column2:
Glucose -> ethanol + carbon dioxide (+ small amount of energy released). This is fermentation.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Photosynthesis (word)
Biology (Triple) · Named biological processes: word and symbol equations
column2:
Carbon dioxide + water -(light energy)-> glucose + oxygen. An endothermic reaction that transfers energy from the environment (light) to the chloroplasts.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Photosynthesis (symbol)
Biology (Triple) · Named biological processes: word and symbol equations
column2:
6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Digestion of starch
Biology (Triple) · Named biological processes: word and symbol equations
column2:
Starch --(amylase)--> maltose --(maltase)--> glucose.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Digestion of protein
Biology (Triple) · Named biological processes: word and symbol equations
column2:
Protein --(protease)--> amino acids.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Digestion of lipids
Biology (Triple) · Named biological processes: word and symbol equations
column2:
Lipids --(lipase)--> fatty acids + glycerol.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Bile function
Biology (Triple) · Named biological processes: word and symbol equations
column2:
Produced by the liver, stored in the gall bladder; neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fats, increasing their surface area for lipase to act on.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Lock and key model
Biology (Triple) · Enzymes and factors affecting activity
column2:
An enzyme's active site has a specific shape that only fits a complementary substrate; this explains why enzymes are specific to one reaction/substrate.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Effect of temperature on enzyme activity
Biology (Triple) · Enzymes and factors affecting activity
column2:
Rate increases as temperature rises (more kinetic energy, more frequent successful collisions) up to the optimum; above the optimum, the enzyme denatures - the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits, so activity falls sharply.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Effect of pH on enzyme activity
Biology (Triple) · Enzymes and factors affecting activity
column2:
Each enzyme has an optimum pH; above or below this, the enzyme denatures as the active site's shape is disrupted by changes in bonding, reducing or stopping activity.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Effect of substrate concentration
Biology (Triple) · Enzymes and factors affecting activity
column2:
Rate increases as substrate concentration increases, because more successful collisions occur between enzyme and substrate, until the enzyme active sites become saturated and rate levels off.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Denaturation
Biology (Triple) · Enzymes and factors affecting activity
column2:
A permanent change to the shape of an enzyme's active site (caused by excess heat or wrong pH) so the substrate can no longer bind and the enzyme stops working.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Amylase
Biology (Triple) · Enzymes and factors affecting activity
column2:
Digestive enzyme that breaks down starch into sugars (maltose); produced in the salivary glands, pancreas and small intestine.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Protease
Biology (Triple) · Enzymes and factors affecting activity
column2:
Digestive enzyme that breaks down proteins into amino acids; produced in the stomach, pancreas and small intestine.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Lipase
Biology (Triple) · Enzymes and factors affecting activity
column2:
Digestive enzyme that breaks down lipids into fatty acids and glycerol; produced in the pancreas and small intestine.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Normal human body temperature
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Approximately 37 degC, the optimum temperature for enzyme activity in the body.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Normal blood glucose regulation - high glucose
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Pancreas detects high blood glucose and secretes insulin; insulin causes liver and muscle cells to take up glucose and store it as glycogen, lowering blood glucose.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Normal blood glucose regulation - low glucose
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Pancreas secretes glucagon, which causes liver cells to convert stored glycogen back into glucose and release it into the blood, raising blood glucose.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Type 1 diabetes
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
The pancreas produces little or no insulin (usually an autoimmune cause); treated with insulin injections.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Type 2 diabetes
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Body cells no longer respond properly to insulin (insulin resistance), often linked to obesity; managed by a carbohydrate-controlled diet, exercise, and sometimes medication.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Insulin: source and effect
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Source: pancreas. Effect: lowers blood glucose by stimulating uptake and storage of glucose as glycogen in liver/muscle cells.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Glucagon: source and effect
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Source: pancreas. Effect: raises blood glucose by stimulating breakdown of glycogen to glucose in the liver.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Adrenaline: source and effect
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Source: adrenal glands. Effect: prepares the body for 'fight or flight' - increases heart rate, boosts blood glucose release, increases blood flow to muscles.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Thyroxine: source and effect
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Source: thyroid gland. Effect: regulates basal metabolic rate, controlled by negative feedback.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
FSH (follicle stimulating hormone): source and effect
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Source: pituitary gland. Effect: causes maturation of an egg in the ovary and stimulates oestrogen production.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
LH (luteinising hormone): source and effect
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Source: pituitary gland. Effect: stimulates the release of the egg (ovulation) at around day 14 of the menstrual cycle.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Oestrogen: source and effect
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Source: ovaries. Effect: causes the uterus lining to thicken/repair, and inhibits FSH while stimulating LH release at high levels.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Progesterone: source and effect
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
Source: ovaries (corpus luteum). Effect: maintains the uterus lining during the cycle/pregnancy, and inhibits FSH and LH.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Negative feedback principle
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
A control system detects a change from the normal level and triggers a response that reverses the change, returning the level towards normal (used for glucose, thyroxine, water balance).

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Osmoregulation - low water level
Biology (Triple) · Homeostasis: reference values and hormones
column2:
More ADH (antidiuretic hormone) is released from the pituitary gland, making the kidney tubules more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed and urine becomes more concentrated.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Quadrat population estimate formula
Biology (Triple) · Ecology sampling and calculations
column2:
Estimated total population = (mean number of organisms per quadrat / area of one quadrat) x total area of habitat.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Why use random sampling
Biology (Triple) · Ecology sampling and calculations
column2:
Random placement of quadrats (e.g. using random coordinates from a grid) avoids bias, so the sample fairly represents the whole habitat.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Percentage cover
Biology (Triple) · Ecology sampling and calculations
column2:
Used for plants that are hard to count individually; estimated using a quadrat divided into a grid, counting the percentage of squares covered by the species.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Transect method
Biology (Triple) · Ecology sampling and calculations
column2:
A line placed across a habitat along an environmental gradient; quadrats are sampled at set intervals along it to show how distribution/abundance changes across the gradient.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Capture-recapture formula (Lincoln index)
Biology (Triple) · Ecology sampling and calculations
column2:
Estimated population size = (number caught in first sample x number caught in second sample) / number in second sample that are marked (recaptured).

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Capture-recapture method requirements
Biology (Triple) · Ecology sampling and calculations
column2:
Marking must not harm or increase predation risk for the animal, marks must not fade before recapture, and enough time must pass for the marked animals to mix randomly back into the population.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Rate of decay/decomposition calculation
Biology (Triple) · Ecology sampling and calculations
column2:
Rate = amount of change (e.g. mass lost, pH change) / time taken. Used in required practical investigations of decay, e.g. milk with lipase or buried plant material.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Factors increasing rate of decay
Biology (Triple) · Ecology sampling and calculations
column2:
Warmer temperature (up to a point, then enzymes in decomposers denature), presence of water/moisture, and available oxygen (for aerobic decomposers).

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Pyramid of biomass efficiency
Biology (Triple) · Ecology sampling and calculations
column2:
Percentage efficiency of biomass transfer = (biomass transferred to next level / biomass available at the level below) x 100; typically only about 10 percent is transferred, the rest lost via respiration, movement, egestion and excretion.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Magnification formula
Biology (Triple) · Microscopy and magnification calculations
column2:
Magnification = size of image / size of real object. Rearrange as needed: image size = magnification x real size, or real size = image size / magnification.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Unit conversion for microscopy: mm to micrometres
Biology (Triple) · Microscopy and magnification calculations
column2:
1 mm = 1000 micrometres (um). Convert all measurements to the same unit before calculating magnification.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Unit conversion for microscopy: micrometres to nanometres
Biology (Triple) · Microscopy and magnification calculations
column2:
1 micrometre (um) = 1000 nanometres (nm).

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Total magnification of a light microscope
Biology (Triple) · Microscopy and magnification calculations
column2:
Total magnification = eyepiece lens magnification x objective lens magnification.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Resolution definition
Biology (Triple) · Microscopy and magnification calculations
column2:
The ability to distinguish between two separate points that are very close together; electron microscopes have much higher resolution than light microscopes, allowing much greater useful magnification.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Why electron microscopes reveal more detail
Biology (Triple) · Microscopy and magnification calculations
column2:
They have a much higher resolution than light microscopes, so they can be used to observe much smaller structures such as ribosomes and internal organelle detail that light microscopes cannot resolve.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Scale bar interpretation
Biology (Triple) · Microscopy and magnification calculations
column2:
A scale bar on a micrograph shows the real-life length represented by a given length on the image; measure the bar and the structure in the same units, then use the ratio to calculate real size.

Biology (Triple) · AQA 8461

column1:
Rearranging the magnification formula for real size
Biology (Triple) · Microscopy and magnification calculations
column2:
Real size = image size / magnification. Always convert image size to the same unit you want the real size in before dividing, e.g. mm to um.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

Flame emission spectroscopy
Chemistry (Triple) · Qualitative analysis: tests and results
