An instrumental method that identifies metal ions from the exact wavelengths of light emitted and their intensity, giving faster, more accurate and more sensitive results than a manual flame test, and working on very small or mixed samples.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Moles from mass
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
moles = mass (g) / relative formula mass (Mr). Use to convert a measured mass into an amount for reacting-mass calculations.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Mass from moles
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
mass (g) = moles x Mr. Use to predict the mass of product or reactant needed.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Concentration (mass basis)
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
concentration (g/dm3) = mass of solute (g) / volume of solution (dm3). Use for making up solutions of known strength.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Concentration (moles basis)
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
concentration (mol/dm3) = moles of solute / volume of solution (dm3). Use for titration and reacting-volume calculations.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Converting cm3 to dm3
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
divide cm3 by 1000 to get dm3. Always convert before using concentration in mol/dm3.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Titration moles calculation
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
moles = concentration (mol/dm3) x volume (dm3). Find moles of the known solution first, use the balanced equation mole ratio to find moles of the unknown, then convert to concentration or mass as needed.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Percentage yield
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
percentage yield = (actual mass of product / theoretical maximum mass of product) x 100. Always less than 100 percent due to incomplete reactions, losses during transfer/filtration, or side reactions.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Atom economy
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
atom economy = (Mr of desired product / sum of Mr of all reactants) x 100. High atom economy means less waste and is important for sustainable industrial processes.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Molar gas volume (RTP)
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm3 (24,000 cm3) at room temperature and pressure (20 degC, 1 atm).

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Moles of gas from volume
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
moles = volume of gas (dm3) / 24. Use for gas volume calculations at RTP, e.g. finding gas produced in a reaction.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Limiting reactant identification
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
Convert all reactant masses to moles, divide each by its balancing number in the equation; the smallest result identifies the limiting reactant.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Relative formula mass (Mr)
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
Sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms shown in the formula, e.g. Mr of CaCO3 = 40 + 12 + (16x3) = 100.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Conservation of mass check
Chemistry (Triple) · Quantitative chemistry formulae
column2:
In a closed system, total mass of reactants = total mass of products; an apparent mass change in an open system usually means a gas has entered or escaped.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Alkanes: general formula
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
CnH2n+2. Saturated hydrocarbons (single C-C bonds only). First four: methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Alkanes: key reaction
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
Complete combustion: alkane + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water. Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) produces carbon monoxide and/or soot (carbon) instead.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Alkenes: general formula
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
CnH2n. Unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one C=C double bond. First three: ethene C2H4, propene C3H6, butene C4H8.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Alkenes: test
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
Shaken with orange bromine water: alkenes decolourise it to colourless via addition across the double bond; alkanes do not change its colour.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Alkenes: key reaction
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
Addition reactions add atoms across the C=C bond, e.g. with hydrogen (forms an alkane), water (forms an alcohol), or a halogen (forms a dihalogenoalkane).

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Alcohols: general formula
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
CnH2n+1OH, functional group -OH. First four: methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Alcohols: key reactions
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
React with sodium to release hydrogen gas; burn in air (combustion) to give CO2 and water; can be oxidised (e.g. by microbial action or oxidising agents) to carboxylic acids.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Alcohols: production
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
Ethanol is made by fermentation of sugar with yeast at 25-35 degC in anaerobic conditions, or industrially by hydration of ethene with a catalyst.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Carboxylic acids: general formula
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
CnH2n+1COOH, functional group -COOH. First four: methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic acid.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Carboxylic acids: properties
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
Weak acids - only partially ionise in water, so react less vigorously than strong acids of the same concentration; react with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Esters: formation
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
Carboxylic acid + alcohol -> ester + water, using an acid catalyst (e.g. concentrated sulfuric acid). Esters have distinctive sweet smells and the functional group -COO-.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Addition polymers
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
Formed when many unsaturated alkene monomers join together, opening their double bonds, with no other product formed, e.g. many ethene -> poly(ethene).

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Condensation polymers
Chemistry (Triple) · Organic chemistry: homologous series
column2:
Formed when monomers with two functional groups join, releasing a small molecule (usually water) at each new bond, e.g. formation of polyesters.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Early atmosphere composition
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Formed from intense volcanic activity releasing mostly carbon dioxide and water vapour, with little or no oxygen, similar to the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
How oceans formed
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
As the Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form the oceans.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
How CO2 decreased
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Carbon dioxide was locked up in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels, and was dissolved into the oceans, then absorbed by algae and plants for photosynthesis.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
How oxygen increased
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Algae and plants evolved and produced oxygen by photosynthesis over billions of years, gradually building up the roughly 21 percent level in today's atmosphere.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Current atmosphere composition
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
About 80 percent nitrogen, about 20 percent oxygen, with small amounts of carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Greenhouse gases
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour absorb infrared radiation reflected from Earth's surface and re-radiate it, keeping the planet warmer than it would otherwise be.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Human activities increasing greenhouse gases
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Burning fossil fuels increases carbon dioxide; agriculture (livestock, rice paddies, landfill) increases methane.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Global climate change consequences
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Rising sea levels, more extreme weather, changing rainfall patterns, and changes in the distribution of species.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Carbon footprint
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases released over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Ways to reduce carbon footprint
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Using more renewable/low-carbon energy, carbon capture and storage, using less energy, and international agreements to cut emissions.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Common atmospheric pollutants from combustion
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Carbon monoxide (toxic, from incomplete combustion), sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (cause acid rain and respiratory problems), particulates (soot, cause global dimming and health problems).

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Finite vs renewable resources
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Finite resources (e.g. crude oil, metal ores) are used faster than they form and will run out; renewable resources (e.g. timber, biofuel crops) are replenished at a comparable rate to their use.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Life cycle assessment stages
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use and operation; disposal at end of life - transport is included at every stage.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Potable water treatment steps
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Choose an appropriate source, filter through wire mesh then sand beds to remove solids, then sterilise with chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.

Chemistry (Triple) · AQA 8462

column1:
Desalination methods
Chemistry (Triple) · Atmosphere and using resources fact bank
column2:
Distillation (evaporate then condense) or reverse osmosis (force water through a membrane); both require large amounts of energy, making them expensive.

Weight
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
W = m x g (weight in N, mass in kg, gravitational field strength in N/kg). Use for any object resting, hanging or falling near Earth.

Work done
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory

W = F x d (work in J, force in N, distance in m, along the line of action of the force). Use whenever a force moves something.

Force applied to a spring
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
F = k x e (force in N, spring constant in N/m, extension in m). Use for springs within their limit of proportionality.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Moment of a force
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
M = F x d (moment in Nm, force in N, perpendicular distance in m). Use for levers, spanners, balancing problems.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Speed (distance-time)
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
v = s / t (speed in m/s, distance in m, time in s). Use for constant speed or to find average speed.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Acceleration
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
a = (v - u) / t (acceleration in m/s^2, final velocity v, initial velocity u in m/s, time in s). Use whenever velocity changes over time.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Newton's second law
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
F = m x a (force in N, mass in kg, acceleration in m/s^2). Use to link a resultant force to acceleration.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Momentum
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
p = m x v (momentum in kg m/s, mass in kg, velocity in m/s). Use for collisions, explosions and conservation of momentum questions.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Kinetic energy
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
Ek = 1/2 x m x v^2 (energy in J, mass in kg, speed in m/s). Use for a moving object's energy store.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Gravitational potential energy
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
Ep = m x g x h (energy in J, mass in kg, g in N/kg, height in m). Use for height changes near Earth's surface.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Elastic potential energy
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
Ee = 1/2 x k x e^2 (energy in J, spring constant in N/m, extension in m). Use only within the limit of proportionality.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Power
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
P = E / t or P = W / t (power in W, energy or work in J, time in s). Use for rate of energy transfer or rate of doing work.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Efficiency
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer (no unit, or x100 for percent). Use to compare useful vs wasted energy.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Wave speed
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
v = f x lambda (speed in m/s, frequency in Hz, wavelength in m). Use for any wave, including sound and light.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Charge flow
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
Q = I x t (charge in coulombs, current in amps, time in s). Use whenever current flows for a given time.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Potential difference (energy)
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
E = Q x V (energy in J, charge in C, potential difference in V). Use for energy transferred by charge moving through a component.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Density
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
rho = m / V (density in kg/m^3, mass in kg, volume in m^3). Required practical equation for regular and irregular solids and liquids.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Distance from speed and time (rearranged)
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
s = v x t. Use to find distance when speed is constant and time is known.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Pressure (solid on surface)
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
P = F / A (pressure in Pa, force in N, area in m^2). Use for a solid pressing on a surface, not for fluids.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Change in thermal energy
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
Delta E = m x c x Delta theta (energy in J, mass in kg, specific heat capacity in J/kg degC, temperature change in degC). Use when temperature changes but no state change occurs.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Energy for a change of state
Physics (Triple) · Equations you must recall from memory
column2:
E = m x L (energy in J, mass in kg, specific latent heat in J/kg). Use only during melting/freezing or boiling/condensing, when temperature stays constant.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Force on a current-carrying conductor
Physics (Triple) · Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
column2:
F = B x I x l (force in N, magnetic flux density in T, current in A, length in m). Use for motor effect problems.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Transformer turns rule
Physics (Triple) · Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
column2:
Vp / Vs = np / ns (primary/secondary potential difference in V, primary/secondary turns). Use for step-up/step-down transformer questions.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Force on a wire in a field (Alt)
Physics (Triple) · Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
column2:
Given on sheet alongside motor effect; combine with F=BIl for full circuit and field questions.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Orbital equations (qualitative)
Physics (Triple) · Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
column2:

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
GPE change with weight given
Physics (Triple) · Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
column2:
When weight is already given rather than mass and g separately, the sheet shows Ep = weight x height for direct substitution.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

Refractive index
Physics (Triple) · Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
column2:
n = sin(angle of incidence) / sin(angle of refraction). Use for light passing between two media in required practical work.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Period of a wave
Physics (Triple) · Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
column2:
T = 1 / f (period in s, frequency in Hz). Given alongside wave speed equation; use to link period and frequency.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Electrical power (two forms)
Physics (Triple) · Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
column2:
P = V x I and P = I^2 x R, both given on sheet. Use P=VI when V and I are known; use I^2R when current and resistance are known and V is not.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Force and change in momentum
Physics (Triple) · Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
column2:
F = (m x delta v) / t (force in N, change in momentum in kg m/s, time in s). Use for impact/safety questions like airbags and seatbelts.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Circular motion period-speed link
Physics (Triple) · Equations given on the AQA physics equation sheet
column2:
For an object in a circular orbit, v = (2 x pi x r) / T (speed in m/s, radius in m, time period T in s). Given on sheet for space physics questions.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Base unit: length
Physics (Triple) · SI units and prefixes
column2:
Metre, m. All distances must be converted to metres before substituting into equations.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

Base unit: mass
Physics (Triple) · SI units and prefixes

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:

The energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius (unit J/kg degC).

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Specific latent heat
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
The energy required to change the state of one kilogram of a substance with no change in temperature (unit J/kg).

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Specific latent heat of fusion
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
The energy needed to change one kilogram of a substance from solid to liquid at its melting point, with no temperature change.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Specific latent heat of vaporisation
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
The energy needed to change one kilogram of a substance from liquid to gas at its boiling point, with no temperature change.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Internal energy
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Pressure
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
Force acting normally (at right angles) per unit area: P = F / A, measured in pascals.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Absolute zero
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
-273 degC (0 K), the temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy and gas pressure would theoretically reach zero.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Atom (nuclear model)
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
A neutral particle with a small, dense, positively charged nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons in shells; atomic radius about 1 x 10^-10 m, nuclear radius about 1 x 10^-14 m.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Isotope
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
Atoms of the same element (same proton number) with a different number of neutrons, so a different mass number.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Ionising radiation
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms it passes through, creating ions.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Activity
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, measured in becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Count rate
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
The number of decays recorded per unit time by a detector, e.g. a Geiger-Muller tube; it is proportional to activity but not identical to it because not all decays are detected.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Half-life
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
The time taken for the number of nuclei of the original isotope in a sample to halve, or for the count rate/activity from a sample to fall to half its initial level.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Irradiation
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
The process of exposing an object to radiation from a source; the object does not become radioactive itself.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Contamination (radioactive)
Physics (Triple) · Key definitions: heat, pressure, radioactivity
column2:
The unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or in another material, which can then continue to emit radiation from within or on that material.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
National Grid purpose
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers, distributing electrical power efficiently around the country.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Why transmit at high voltage
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
For a fixed power, higher transmission voltage means lower current; since power loss to heat in cables is I^2 x R, lower current greatly reduces energy wasted.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Step-up transformer
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Located at the power station; increases voltage and decreases current for efficient transmission.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Step-down transformer
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Located near consumers (local substations); decreases voltage to a safe, usable level, e.g. 230 V mains in the UK.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Renewable energy resources
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Wind, solar, geothermal, hydroelectric, tidal, wave and biofuel; resources that are replenished as they are used, at a rate comparable to consumption.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Non-renewable energy resources
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear fuel; resources that will eventually run out because they form far slower than they are used.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Wind power
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Turbines convert kinetic energy of moving air into electrical energy; no fuel cost or pollution, but unreliable and can spoil the landscape.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Solar power
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Photovoltaic cells convert light directly into electricity; reliable in daylight, no pollution when running, but output is low on cloudy days or at night.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Hydroelectric power
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Water stored in a reservoir is released through turbines; reliable and quick to respond to demand, but has high initial environmental and construction impact.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Tidal power
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Uses the rise and fall of tides to drive turbines; predictable timing but not constant power, and can affect estuary ecosystems.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Nuclear power
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Uses fission of uranium or plutonium to heat water and drive turbines; low running carbon emissions but produces radioactive waste and has high decommissioning costs.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Fossil fuels
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Coal, oil and gas release energy on combustion; reliable and high output, but release carbon dioxide (contributing to global warming) and other pollutants.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Trend in UK energy use
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Increasing use of renewables and gas, decreasing use of coal, aiming to reduce carbon dioxide emissions over time.

Physics (Triple) · AQA 8463

column1:
Energy demand and supply matching
Physics (Triple) · National Grid and energy resources fact bank
column2:
Power stations must be able to respond quickly to changes in demand; pumped storage hydroelectric schemes provide rapid-response backup.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Tectonic hazard, developed country example
Geography · Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
column2:
The Kaikoura earthquake, New Zealand, magnitude 7.8, struck on 14 November 2016, killing 2 people and causing about NZ$2 billion of damage, with strong building codes limiting casualties.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Tectonic hazard, developing/emerging country example
Geography · Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
column2:
The Haiti earthquake, magnitude 7.0, struck on 12 January 2010 near Port-au-Prince, killing an estimated 160,000-230,000 people due to poor building standards and weak emergency response.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Development case study: India
Geography · Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
column2:
India's GNI per capita was around US$2,390 (World Bank, Atlas method, recent data) with an HDI around 0.64 (medium-high), showing rapid IT and service-sector growth (e.g. Bangalore) alongside continued rural poverty.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Urbanisation case study: Mumbai
Geography · Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
column2:
Mumbai's population is around 20 million in its metropolitan area; Dharavi, one of its largest informal settlements, houses an estimated 700,000-1 million people in about 2.1 square kilometres.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
UK city case study: Birmingham
Geography · Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
column2:
Birmingham, UK's second largest city (population approximately 1.15 million), lost tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs from deindustrialisation from the 1970s-1990s, followed by regeneration schemes such as the Bullring (opened 2003) and HS2-linked investment.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Coastal management case study: Holderness coast
Geography · Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
column2:
The Holderness coast, East Yorkshire, erodes at an average rate of about 1.5-2 metres per year, among the fastest eroding coastlines in Europe; Mappleton has been protected since 1991 with rock groynes and a rock revetment.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
River management case study: UK
Geography · Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
column2:
The River Cherwell/Banbury flood scheme, or similarly the River Skerne, Darlington (naturalisation scheme, 1990s), used soft engineering to restore a meandering channel and floodplain storage to reduce downstream flood risk.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Rainforest case study: deforestation
Geography · Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
column2:
The Amazon rainforest lost roughly 11,000 square kilometres of forest cover in Brazil in a recent reported year (INPE data), driven mainly by cattle ranching and soy farming.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Taiga/energy resource case study
Geography · Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
column2:
Alberta's Athabasca tar sands, Canada, produce over 3 million barrels of oil per day using energy-intensive extraction, generating higher carbon emissions per barrel than conventional oil.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Global biome distribution located example
Geography · Named case studies and located examples (one item each, with figures and dates)
column2:
The Sahara Desert biome (around 30 degrees N, area approximately 9.2 million square kilometres) sits under the descending, high-pressure limb of the Hadley cell, giving very low rainfall.

column1:

The difference in standards of living and wellbeing between the richest and poorest countries or regions in the world.

Sustainable development

Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Biodiversity

column2:
The variety of plant and animal life in a particular habitat or ecosystem.

column1:
Energy security

column2:
Uninterrupted access to sufficient, affordable and reliable energy supplies to meet a country's needs.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:

column2:

column1:

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Discharge
Geography · Definitions glossary
column2:
The volume of water flowing through a river cross-section per second, measured in cumecs (cubic metres per second).

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:

column2:
The decline of manufacturing industry and its associated employment in a country or region.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

A structured investigation of a geographical question using primary data collected in the field and secondary data, followed by analysis and evaluation.

column2:
Add all the values together and divide by the number of values. Sensitive to extreme values (outliers).

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Median
Geography · Statistics skills for fieldwork and data
column2:
Put the values in order; the middle value (or mean of the two middle values if an even number of data points). Not affected by outliers.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Mode
Geography · Statistics skills for fieldwork and data
column2:
The value that occurs most often in the data set. Useful for categorical data.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Range
Geography · Statistics skills for fieldwork and data
column2:
Highest value minus lowest value; a simple measure of spread, but very sensitive to outliers.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Interquartile range (IQR)
Geography · Statistics skills for fieldwork and data
column2:
Upper quartile minus lower quartile; measures the spread of the middle 50% of data and is less affected by outliers than the range.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Spearman's rank correlation, in words
Geography · Statistics skills for fieldwork and data
column2:
Rank both data sets separately, find the difference in rank for each pair, square each difference, sum the squared differences, then apply the formula to give a value between -1 and +1 showing the strength and direction of correlation.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

Geography · Statistics skills for fieldwork and data
column2:
A result close to +1 shows strong positive correlation, close to -1 shows strong negative correlation, and close to 0 shows little or no correlation; always state what this means in the geographical context.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Anomalies in data
Geography · Statistics skills for fieldwork and data
column2:
A data point that does not fit the general pattern; identify it, suggest a geographical or methodological reason for it, and consider whether to exclude it from analysis.

Geography · Pearson Edexcel B 1GB0

column1:
Why use inter-quartile range over range for fieldwork data
Geography · Statistics skills for fieldwork and data
column2:
IQR removes the influence of one or two extreme results (outliers) caused by measurement error or unusual local conditions, giving a fairer picture of typical spread.

column1:
Energy value of alcohol
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Energy values per gram and BMR, PAL and energy balance
column2:
Provides 7 kcal per gram - not a nutrient, but relevant to overall energy intake.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate)
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Energy values per gram and BMR, PAL and energy balance
column2:
The minimum amount of energy the body needs at rest to maintain vital functions such as breathing, circulation and cell repair.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
PAL (Physical Activity Level)
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Energy values per gram and BMR, PAL and energy balance
column2:
A measure of how active a person is; a higher PAL means more energy used through activity and therefore higher total energy needs on top of BMR.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Energy balance
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Energy values per gram and BMR, PAL and energy balance
column2:
The relationship between energy consumed from food and drink and energy expended through BMR and physical activity; a balanced state maintains stable body weight.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Positive energy balance
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Energy values per gram and BMR, PAL and energy balance
column2:
When energy intake is greater than energy output, leading to weight gain over time as excess energy is stored as fat.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Negative energy balance
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Energy values per gram and BMR, PAL and energy balance
column2:
When energy intake is less than energy output, leading to weight loss over time as the body uses stored energy reserves.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Energy dense foods
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Energy values per gram and BMR, PAL and energy balance
column2:
Foods that provide a large amount of energy (calories) in a small portion, typically high in fat and/or sugar, such as crisps, chocolate and fried food.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Factors affecting energy needs
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Energy values per gram and BMR, PAL and energy balance
column2:
Age, gender, body size, growth stage (e.g. higher needs in teenagers) and PAL all affect an individual's total energy requirement.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Coagulation
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Functional and chemical properties glossary
column2:
The change of a protein from a liquid to a solid or semi-solid state on heating, which cannot be reversed. Food example: egg white turning solid when fried or boiled.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Denaturation
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Functional and chemical properties glossary
column2:
A permanent change to the structure of a protein caused by heat, acid or mechanical action (such as whisking), altering its shape and properties. Food example: whisking egg white to make meringue.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Gelatinisation
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Functional and chemical properties glossary
column2:
Starch granules absorbing liquid and swelling when heated, causing a mixture to thicken. Food example: a roux-based white sauce thickening as it is heated.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Dextrinisation
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Functional and chemical properties glossary
column2:
Dry heat breaking down starch on the surface of a food into dextrins, causing it to brown and change flavour. Food example: the browning of toasted bread.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Caramelisation
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Functional and chemical properties glossary
column2:
Sugar breaking down under heat, changing colour to brown and developing a nutty, sweet flavour. Food example: sugar melted and heated to make caramel sauce.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Emulsification
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Functional and chemical properties glossary
column2:
Combining two liquids that would normally separate, such as oil and water, using an emulsifier to stabilise the mixture. Food example: egg yolk lecithin binding oil and vinegar in mayonnaise.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Plasticity
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Functional and chemical properties glossary
column2:
The ability of a fat to be spread, moulded or creamed at room temperature without melting completely. Food example: butter being creamed with sugar for a cake mixture.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Shortening
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Functional and chemical properties glossary
column2:
Fat coating flour particles during preparation, preventing long strands of gluten forming and giving a short, crumbly texture. Food example: butter rubbed into flour for shortcrust pastry.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Aeration
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Functional and chemical properties glossary
column2:
Incorporating air into a mixture, by whisking, creaming, folding, sieving or rubbing in, to create a lighter texture. Food example: whisking egg and sugar together to aerate a sponge cake mixture.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Foams
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Functional and chemical properties glossary
column2:
A structure formed when air is trapped within a liquid or semi-solid, often stabilised by protein. Food example: whisked egg white forming a foam for meringue or mousse.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Conduction
Food Preparation and Nutrition · The four heat transfer methods with examples
column2:
Heat travels through direct contact between particles, from a heat source through equipment into the food. Example: heat passing from a hob through a metal saucepan base into boiling potatoes.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Convection
Food Preparation and Nutrition · The four heat transfer methods with examples
column2:
Heat travels through the movement of currents in a liquid or gas (air); hot currents rise and cooler currents sink, circulating heat. Example: hot air circulating in a fan oven to bake a cake, or currents circulating heat through boiling water.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Radiation
Food Preparation and Nutrition · The four heat transfer methods with examples
column2:
Heat travels directly as electromagnetic waves from the heat source to the food, without needing a solid or liquid medium. Example: heat from a grill element browning the top of a cheese-topped dish, or a toaster.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Microwave (electromagnetic radiation)
Food Preparation and Nutrition · The four heat transfer methods with examples
column2:
Microwaves penetrate food and cause water molecules within it to vibrate rapidly, generating heat from within through friction. Example: reheating a ready meal in a microwave oven.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Conduction in liquids
Food Preparation and Nutrition · The four heat transfer methods with examples
column2:
Heat also conducts between adjacent liquid particles in direct contact, though in most cooking liquids convection currents dominate once the liquid begins to move.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Conduction and pan material
Food Preparation and Nutrition · The four heat transfer methods with examples
column2:
Metals such as copper and aluminium conduct heat quickly and evenly, giving faster, more controllable cooking; poor conductors like glass heat more slowly and unevenly.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Convection in an oven
Food Preparation and Nutrition · The four heat transfer methods with examples
column2:
In a conventional oven, heat rises from the element, warming air which circulates by convection; a fan oven forces this circulation, cooking food faster and more evenly.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Radiation and browning
Food Preparation and Nutrition · The four heat transfer methods with examples
column2:
Radiant heat from a grill or barbecue cooks the surface of food directly and quickly, producing browning and charring, but does not penetrate deep into thick food as effectively as conduction or convection.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Density and heat transfer rate
Food Preparation and Nutrition · The four heat transfer methods with examples
column2:
Denser foods (e.g. a whole potato) transfer heat more slowly through their structure than less dense foods (e.g. a sliced vegetable), so they take longer to cook through.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Moisture content and heat transfer rate
Food Preparation and Nutrition · The four heat transfer methods with examples
column2:
Foods with higher moisture content generally heat more slowly than dry foods, since energy is used to heat the water and, at boiling point, to convert it to steam.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Fridge temperature
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
Should be kept between 0 and 5 degrees Celsius to slow bacterial growth.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Freezer temperature
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
Should be kept at -18 degrees Celsius or below; bacteria become dormant but are not killed.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Temperature danger zone
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
5 to 63 degrees Celsius; the range in which food poisoning bacteria multiply fastest, with 37 degrees Celsius (body temperature) being optimum for growth.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Core cooking/reheating temperature
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
High-risk food should reach a core temperature of at least 75 degrees Celsius, checked with a temperature probe, and food should only be reheated once.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Hot holding temperature
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
Cooked food that is not served immediately should be kept above 63 degrees Celsius to prevent bacterial growth.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Chilling time after cooking
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
Cooked food that is to be stored should be cooled and refrigerated within 90 minutes to limit time in the danger zone.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
The four Cs: Cleaning
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
Washing hands, equipment and surfaces regularly and thoroughly to prevent the spread of bacteria.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
The four Cs: Cooking
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
Cooking food thoroughly to the correct core temperature (at least 75 degrees Celsius for high-risk food) to kill harmful bacteria.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
The four Cs: Chilling
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
Keeping food that needs to be refrigerated at the correct cold temperature (0 to 5 degrees Celsius) to slow bacterial growth.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
The four Cs: Cross-contamination (avoiding)
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
Keeping raw and ready-to-eat food, and the equipment used for each, separate to stop harmful bacteria spreading.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
High-risk foods
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
Foods that are moist and high in protein, supporting rapid bacterial growth, such as cooked meat and poultry, dairy, eggs, fish, shellfish and cooked rice.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Use-by date
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
A legal safety date; food must not be eaten after this date even if it looks and smells fine, as harmful bacteria may be present.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585

column1:
Best-before date
Food Preparation and Nutrition · Food safety temperatures and the four Cs
column2:
A quality date, not a safety date; food may still be safe to eat after this date but may not be at its best flavour or texture.

Food Preparation and Nutrition · AQA 8585
